nodes.title: A Mathematical Theory of Communication
nodes.authors: C. E. Shannon
nodes.before: Language was studied as grammar and meaning, not as a measurable signal.
nodes.problem: No way to quantify how predictable a stretch of text is.
nodes.breakthrough: Entropy, and the idea that a text source can be modelled as a probability distribution over the next symbol.
nodes.why: Every language model since scores itself on how surprised it is by the next token. That is Shannon's measure.
nodes.next: Statistical speech recognition and machine translation at IBM through the 1970s-80s.
nodes.inherits: Cross-entropy loss, perplexity, and the framing of language as prediction.

nodes.title: A Statistical Approach to Machine Translation
nodes.authors: P. Brown, J. Cocke, S. Della Pietra, V. Della Pietra, F. Jelinek, J. Lafferty, R. Mercer, P. Roossin
nodes.before: Translation systems were hand-built rule sets, one language pair at a time.
nodes.problem: Rules could not cover the variety of real sentences and did not transfer between languages.
nodes.breakthrough: Treat translation as a probability problem learned from aligned corpora rather than a rule problem.
nodes.why: It moved the whole field from hand-written knowledge to learned statistics, the assumption everything later rests on.
nodes.next: Class-based n-grams, then two decades of statistical MT that neural translation eventually displaced.
nodes.inherits: The conviction that data beats hand-crafted rules.

nodes.title: Finding Structure in Time
nodes.authors: Jeffrey L. Elman
nodes.before: Neural nets processed fixed-size inputs with no notion of order.
nodes.problem: Language arrives as a sequence, and context from earlier words has to persist.
nodes.breakthrough: A recurrent hidden layer that feeds its own previous state back in, giving the network a memory of what came before.
nodes.why: It established that sequence can live in a network's internal state rather than in its input window.
nodes.next: LSTM fixed the gradient problems this design exposed.
nodes.inherits: The idea of a running hidden state summarising everything read so far.

nodes.title: Adaptive Mixtures of Local Experts
nodes.authors: R. Jacobs, M. Jordan, S. Nowlan, G. Hinton
nodes.before: One network had to learn every part of a task with the same parameters.
nodes.problem: Different regions of a problem want different specialists, and one dense model spends all its capacity on all of it.
nodes.breakthrough: Several expert subnetworks plus a gating network that decides which expert handles which input.
nodes.why: This is the ancestor of every sparse mixture-of-experts model, including Mixtral, DeepSeek and Llama 4.
nodes.next: Dormant for 25 years until Shazeer scaled it in 2017.
nodes.inherits: Conditional computation: activate a fraction of the parameters per token.

nodes.title: Class-Based n-gram Models of Natural Language
nodes.authors: P. Brown, V. Della Pietra, P. deSouza, J. Lai, R. Mercer
nodes.before: n-gram models counted exact word sequences and assigned zero probability to anything unseen.
nodes.problem: Sparsity: most word sequences never appear in any corpus, however large.
nodes.breakthrough: Cluster words into classes automatically, so statistics are shared between similar words.
nodes.why: The first practical answer to sparsity by grouping words that behave alike, an idea embeddings later generalised.
nodes.next: Bengio's neural language model replaced discrete classes with continuous vectors.
nodes.inherits: The instinct that similar words should share statistical strength.

nodes.title: Long Short-Term Memory
nodes.authors: S. Hochreiter, J. Schmidhuber
nodes.before: Recurrent nets existed but gradients vanished over long sequences, so they forgot.
nodes.problem: Errors propagated backwards through many steps shrink to nothing, capping memory at a few words.
nodes.breakthrough: A gated memory cell that can hold a value unchanged across many steps until a gate decides to alter it.
nodes.why: It made recurrent networks actually usable, and powered sequence learning until attention displaced it.
nodes.next: Seq2seq, neural translation, and ELMo were all built from LSTMs.
nodes.inherits: Gating as a way to control what information persists, and the long-range dependency problem attention later solved differently.

nodes.title: A Neural Probabilistic Language Model
nodes.authors: Y. Bengio, R. Ducharme, P. Vincent, C. Jauvin
nodes.before: Language models counted discrete n-grams, with smoothing to patch the gaps.
nodes.problem: The curse of dimensionality: the number of possible word sequences grows faster than any corpus can cover.
nodes.breakthrough: Learn a continuous vector per word jointly with the language model, so unseen sequences inherit probability from similar ones.
nodes.why: The first model where meaning lives in learned geometry. Every embedding layer in every LLM descends from this.
nodes.next: Word2vec made these vectors cheap enough to compute at scale.
nodes.inherits: Distributed word representations trained by next-word prediction.

nodes.title: Recurrent neural network based language model
nodes.authors: T. Mikolov, M. Karafiát, L. Burget, J. Černocký, S. Khudanpur
nodes.inst: Brno Univ. of Technology / Johns Hopkins
nodes.before: Neural language models used a fixed window of previous words.
nodes.problem: A fixed window cannot carry context from arbitrarily far back.
nodes.breakthrough: Use a recurrent net as the language model, so context is unbounded in principle. Roughly halved perplexity against backoff n-grams.
nodes.why: It proved neural language models beat the statistical state of the art on a real task, not just in theory.
nodes.next: The same author's word2vec, and the seq2seq line.
nodes.inherits: The neural language model as a serious competitor rather than a curiosity.

nodes.title: Natural Language Processing (Almost) from Scratch
nodes.authors: R. Collobert, J. Weston, L. Bottou, M. Karlen, K. Kavukcuoglu, P. Kuksa
nodes.before: Each NLP task had its own pipeline of hand-engineered features.
nodes.problem: Feature engineering did not transfer between tasks and capped accuracy.
nodes.breakthrough: One network, trained on unlabelled text, producing representations that serve many tasks at once.
nodes.why: An early statement of the idea that became pretraining: learn general representations first, specialise later.
nodes.next: Word2vec, then ELMo and BERT, made the idea work at scale.
nodes.inherits: Unsupervised pretraining followed by task-specific use.

nodes.title: Efficient Estimation of Word Representations in Vector Space
nodes.authors: T. Mikolov, K. Chen, G. Corrado, J. Dean
nodes.before: Word vectors existed but training them meant running an expensive neural language model.
nodes.problem: Nobody could afford good embeddings over billions of words.
nodes.breakthrough: Strip the model to a shallow objective, predicting context from a word or vice versa. Quality vectors from 1.6 billion words in under a day.
nodes.why: Embeddings became a commodity, and the geometry of meaning became something you could inspect and reason about.
nodes.next: GloVe, then contextual embeddings from ELMo and BERT.
nodes.inherits: The vector-space view of meaning that underpins retrieval and RAG.

nodes.title: Learning Phrase Representations using RNN Encoder-Decoder
nodes.authors: K. Cho, B. van Merriënboer, C. Gulcehre, D. Bahdanau, F. Bougares, H. Schwenk, Y. Bengio
nodes.before: Neural nets scored translations produced by statistical systems.
nodes.problem: No neural architecture mapped a whole variable-length sentence to another.
nodes.breakthrough: An encoder RNN compressing a sentence into a vector and a decoder RNN generating from it, with a simplified gated unit.
nodes.why: It set up the encoder-decoder frame, and the bottleneck it exposed is what attention was invented to fix.
nodes.next: Bahdanau attention, by an author of this paper, removed the bottleneck a few months later.
nodes.inherits: The encoder-decoder shape still used for translation and, in modified form, T5.

nodes.title: Neural Machine Translation by Jointly Learning to Align and Translate
nodes.authors: D. Bahdanau, K. Cho, Y. Bengio
nodes.before: Seq2seq squeezed an entire source sentence into one fixed-length vector.
nodes.problem: That vector is a bottleneck. Translation quality collapsed on long sentences.
nodes.breakthrough: Let the decoder look back over all encoder states and weight them by relevance at each output step.
nodes.why: Attention starts here, not in 2017. The Transformer generalised this mechanism rather than inventing it.
nodes.next: Luong's variants, then the Transformer, which kept attention and threw away the recurrence.
nodes.inherits: The core operation of every model in use today: a learned, weighted look over other positions.

nodes.title: Sequence to Sequence Learning with Neural Networks
nodes.authors: I. Sutskever, O. Vinyals, Q. Le
nodes.before: Translation was a pipeline of alignment models, phrase tables and reranking.
nodes.problem: No single trainable model took a sentence in and produced a sentence out.
nodes.breakthrough: Two stacked LSTMs, one reading and one writing, trained end to end on pairs.
nodes.why: Generation became a learned mapping rather than an assembled pipeline. This is the direct ancestor of prompt-in, text-out.
nodes.next: Attention was added within the year, and the Transformer replaced the recurrence three years later.
nodes.inherits: End-to-end sequence generation as the basic shape of the task.

nodes.title: GloVe: Global Vectors for Word Representation
nodes.authors: J. Pennington, R. Socher, C. Manning
nodes.before: word2vec learned from local context windows, one sample at a time.
nodes.problem: Local windows ignore the global co-occurrence statistics of the whole corpus.
nodes.breakthrough: Factorise the global word co-occurrence matrix directly, giving vectors with a cleaner interpretation.
nodes.why: It gave the embedding idea a second, complementary derivation and became the default pretrained vectors for years.
nodes.next: Absorbed into ELMo and other models as an input layer.
nodes.inherits: Count-based and predictive embeddings as two views of the same geometry.

nodes.title: Adam: A Method for Stochastic Optimization
nodes.authors: D. Kingma, J. Ba
nodes.before: Training used SGD with hand-tuned learning-rate schedules per task.
nodes.problem: Learning rates that suit one parameter suit another badly, and tuning was fragile.
nodes.breakthrough: Per-parameter adaptive step sizes from running estimates of gradient mean and variance.
nodes.why: Almost every transformer since has been trained with Adam or a close variant. It removed a whole class of tuning failure.
nodes.next: AdamW, and the optimizer-state sharding that ZeRO later required.
nodes.inherits: The default optimizer of the field.

nodes.title: Effective Approaches to Attention-based Neural Machine Translation
nodes.authors: M. Luong, H. Pham, C. Manning
nodes.before: One formulation of attention existed, using a small feed-forward scoring network.
nodes.problem: That scoring step was expensive and its design choices untested.
nodes.breakthrough: Simpler multiplicative scoring, plus global and local attention variants, compared systematically.
nodes.why: The dot-product scoring the Transformer uses comes from this line of simplification.
nodes.next: Scaled dot-product attention in the Transformer.
nodes.inherits: Dot-product similarity as the scoring function inside attention.

nodes.title: Neural Machine Translation of Rare Words with Subword Units
nodes.authors: R. Sennrich, B. Haddow, A. Birch
nodes.before: Models had a fixed word vocabulary and an unknown token for everything else.
nodes.problem: Rare words, names, morphology and other languages fell outside the vocabulary entirely.
nodes.breakthrough: Byte-pair encoding: merge frequent character pairs to build a subword vocabulary that can spell anything.
nodes.why: This is why your tokenizer splits words into pieces, and why models count letters badly and handle numbers oddly.
nodes.next: WordPiece in GNMT, SentencePiece, and the byte-level BPE in GPT-2 onwards.
nodes.inherits: Subword tokenization, still the input layer of essentially every LLM.

nodes.title: Semi-supervised Sequence Learning
nodes.authors: A. Dai, Q. Le
nodes.before: Sequence models were trained from scratch on each labelled task.
nodes.problem: Labelled data is scarce; unlabelled text is not.
nodes.breakthrough: Pretrain a recurrent model as a language model or autoencoder, then fine-tune it on the target task.
nodes.why: The pretrain-then-fine-tune recipe in its original form. GPT-1 and BERT both cite it.
nodes.next: ULMFiT, ELMo, GPT-1 and BERT built directly on this template.
nodes.inherits: The two-stage training that defines modern LLM development.

nodes.title: Deep Residual Learning for Image Recognition
nodes.authors: K. He, X. Zhang, S. Ren, J. Sun
nodes.before: Adding layers past a certain depth made networks worse, not better.
nodes.problem: Gradients degrade through long stacks of transformations.
nodes.breakthrough: Add the input of a block to its output, so the block only has to learn a correction.
nodes.why: A vision paper, but every transformer block is wrapped in residual connections. Without them, depth does not train.
nodes.next: Adopted wholesale by the Transformer and everything after it.
nodes.inherits: The skip connection around every attention and feed-forward sublayer.

nodes.title: Layer Normalization
nodes.authors: J. Ba, J. Kiros, G. Hinton
nodes.before: Batch normalisation stabilised training but depended on batch statistics.
nodes.problem: Batch statistics are awkward for variable-length sequences and small batches.
nodes.breakthrough: Normalise across the features of each example independently of the batch.
nodes.why: The other half of the transformer block's plumbing. Pre-norm placement is what makes deep stacks trainable.
nodes.next: Used in the Transformer, then moved before each sublayer in GPT-2.
nodes.inherits: The normalisation layer inside every transformer block.

nodes.title: Google's Neural Machine Translation System
nodes.authors: Y. Wu, M. Schuster, Z. Chen, et al. (31 authors)
nodes.before: Neural translation worked in papers; production systems were still statistical.
nodes.problem: Research models were too slow and too brittle to serve at Google scale.
nodes.breakthrough: A deep LSTM encoder-decoder with attention, wordpiece tokenization and the engineering to deploy it.
nodes.why: The first time a neural sequence model replaced a mature statistical system in a product used by millions.
nodes.next: The Transformer, from the same organisation, made this architecture obsolete within a year.
nodes.inherits: WordPiece tokenization, and the proof that neural generation can ship.

nodes.title: Outrageously Large Neural Networks: The Sparsely-Gated Mixture-of-Experts Layer
nodes.authors: N. Shazeer, A. Mirhoseini, K. Maziarz, A. Davis, Q. Le, G. Hinton, J. Dean
nodes.before: Model capacity and compute per example rose together, so bigger meant slower.
nodes.problem: You cannot afford to run every parameter on every token.
nodes.breakthrough: Thousands of expert subnetworks with a gate selecting a few per token, adding capacity without adding compute.
nodes.why: It revived the 1991 mixture-of-experts idea at scale and set up GShard, Switch, Mixtral and the DeepSeek line.
nodes.next: GShard and Switch Transformer industrialised the routing.
nodes.inherits: Sparse activation, now standard in frontier models.

nodes.title: Billion-scale similarity search with GPUs
nodes.authors: J. Johnson, M. Douze, H. Jégou
nodes.before: Similarity search over large vector sets ran on CPU and did not scale.
nodes.problem: Retrieval over billions of embeddings was too slow to sit inside a model's loop.
nodes.breakthrough: GPU-accelerated approximate nearest-neighbour search, released as a library.
nodes.why: The plumbing under every vector database and RAG stack. DPR and RAG both call it directly.
nodes.next: DPR and RAG used it; the commercial vector-database market grew around the same primitive.
nodes.inherits: Fast approximate vector search as an assumed capability.

nodes.title: Convolutional Sequence to Sequence Learning
nodes.authors: J. Gehring, M. Auli, D. Grangier, D. Yarats, Y. Dauphin
nodes.before: Sequence models were recurrent, and recurrence forced sequential computation.
nodes.problem: Training could not be parallelised across positions, so it was slow.
nodes.breakthrough: Replace recurrence with stacked convolutions plus attention at every layer.
nodes.why: The road not taken. It showed removing recurrence was possible months before the Transformer did it differently.
nodes.next: The Transformer cited it and then overtook it comprehensively.
nodes.inherits: Mostly historical: it marks that parallelism, not attention alone, was the prize.

nodes.title: Deep Reinforcement Learning from Human Preferences
nodes.authors: P. Christiano, J. Leike, T. Brown, M. Martic, S. Legg, D. Amodei
nodes.before: Reinforcement learning needed a hand-written reward function.
nodes.problem: Many goals are easy to judge and hard to specify. You know good behaviour when you see it.
nodes.breakthrough: Learn a reward model from human comparisons between pairs of behaviours, then optimise against it.
nodes.why: The whole alignment stack starts here. InstructGPT, ChatGPT and Claude are this method applied to language.
nodes.next: Ziegler applied it to language models in 2019, then summarisation, then instruction following.
nodes.inherits: Reward models learned from preference comparisons.

nodes.title: Attention Is All You Need
nodes.authors: A. Vaswani, N. Shazeer, N. Parmar, J. Uszkoreit, L. Jones, A. Gomez, Ł. Kaiser, I. Polosukhin
nodes.inst: Google Brain / Google Research / U. Toronto
nodes.before: Attention was a component bolted onto recurrent encoder-decoders.
nodes.problem: Recurrence forces computation in sequence, which wastes GPUs and limits how far back a model can reliably look.
nodes.breakthrough: Remove recurrence entirely. Self-attention lets every position attend to every other in one parallel operation, with multi-head projections and positional encodings to restore order.
nodes.why: This is the substrate everything since runs on. Not because attention was new, but because removing recurrence made scale affordable.
nodes.next: GPT-1 took the decoder, BERT took the encoder, and the split defined the next five years.
nodes.inherits: The architecture itself, essentially unchanged in outline since 2017.

nodes.title: Learned in Translation: Contextualized Word Vectors
nodes.authors: B. McCann, J. Bradbury, C. Xiong, R. Socher
nodes.before: Every word had one vector regardless of the sentence it appeared in.
nodes.problem: Bank in a river sentence and bank in a finance sentence got identical representations.
nodes.breakthrough: Take the encoder from a trained translation model and use its hidden states as context-sensitive word vectors.
nodes.why: The first workable contextual embedding, a few months before ELMo made the idea famous.
nodes.next: ELMo did the same thing from a language model instead of a translation model, and did it better.
nodes.inherits: The principle that a word's representation should depend on its context.

nodes.title: Mixed Precision Training
nodes.authors: P. Micikevicius, et al. (10 authors)
nodes.before: Training ran in 32-bit floating point throughout.
nodes.problem: Memory and bandwidth, not arithmetic, were the binding constraints on model size.
nodes.breakthrough: Keep weights in 16-bit for the forward and backward pass, with loss scaling and a 32-bit master copy for stability.
nodes.why: It roughly halved the memory cost of training, which is part of why billion-parameter models became affordable.
nodes.next: Megatron, ZeRO and every large training run since depend on it.
nodes.inherits: Reduced precision as the default, now extended to bf16 and fp8.

nodes.title: Universal Language Model Fine-tuning for Text Classification
nodes.authors: J. Howard, S. Ruder
nodes.before: Pretraining helped, but fine-tuning often destroyed what pretraining had learned.
nodes.problem: Naive fine-tuning causes catastrophic forgetting of general knowledge.
nodes.breakthrough: A fine-tuning recipe: gradual unfreezing, discriminative learning rates per layer, and a shaped schedule.
nodes.why: It made transfer learning reliable for text and put the pretrain-fine-tune loop in mainstream practice.
nodes.next: GPT-1 and BERT arrived within the year and absorbed the practice.
nodes.inherits: The fine-tuning craft that LoRA and QLoRA later made cheap.

nodes.title: Deep Contextualized Word Representations
nodes.authors: M. Peters, M. Neumann, M. Iyyer, M. Gardner, C. Clark, K. Lee, L. Zettlemoyer
nodes.before: Static embeddings like word2vec and GloVe were the standard input layer.
nodes.problem: One vector per word cannot represent sense, syntax or reference, all of which depend on context.
nodes.breakthrough: Run a deep bidirectional LSTM language model and use its internal layers as the word representation.
nodes.why: It broke the static-embedding era and showed that a pretrained language model is a general-purpose feature extractor.
nodes.next: BERT replaced the LSTM with a Transformer encoder months later.
nodes.inherits: Contextual representations, now simply what a model's hidden states are.

nodes.title: Improving Language Understanding by Generative Pre-Training
nodes.authors: A. Radford, K. Narasimhan, T. Salimans, I. Sutskever
nodes.before: Pretraining was done with recurrent models and mostly produced features, not generators.
nodes.problem: Could a single generative pretrained model be adapted to many understanding tasks?
nodes.breakthrough: Pretrain a Transformer decoder on plain text with next-token prediction, then fine-tune with a task head.
nodes.why: The decoder-only bet. Unfashionable next to BERT at the time, and the line that led to everything from GPT-3 onward.
nodes.next: GPT-2 scaled it and dropped the fine-tuning step for many tasks.
nodes.inherits: The architecture and objective of every modern LLM.

nodes.title: SentencePiece: A simple and language independent subword tokenizer
nodes.authors: T. Kudo, J. Richardson
nodes.before: Subword tokenizers assumed text was already split into words by whitespace.
nodes.problem: That assumption fails for Japanese, Chinese, Thai and any language without spaces.
nodes.breakthrough: Treat raw text, spaces included, as the input and learn subwords directly from it, reversibly.
nodes.why: It made tokenization language-agnostic, which is why multilingual models are practical.
nodes.next: Used by T5, Llama and most non-English-first models.
nodes.inherits: The tokenizer library much of the field still uses.

nodes.title: BERT: Pre-training of Deep Bidirectional Transformers
nodes.authors: J. Devlin, M. Chang, K. Lee, K. Toutanova
nodes.before: Pretrained language models read left to right, because prediction requires it.
nodes.problem: For understanding tasks, the words after a position matter as much as those before.
nodes.breakthrough: Mask random tokens and predict them from both directions, so every layer sees full context. GLUE rose to 80.5.
nodes.why: It dominated NLP for three years and still powers embeddings and retrieval, even though generation went the other way.
nodes.next: RoBERTa tuned the recipe; the encoder line fed Sentence-BERT, DPR and modern retrieval.
nodes.inherits: The encoder half of the field: embeddings, rerankers, classifiers.

nodes.title: Transformer-XL: Attentive Language Models Beyond a Fixed-Length Context
nodes.authors: Z. Dai, Z. Yang, Y. Yang, J. Carbonell, Q. Le, R. Salakhutdinov
nodes.before: Transformers processed fixed segments with no memory between them.
nodes.problem: Context was capped by the segment, and text was chopped arbitrarily at segment boundaries.
nodes.breakthrough: Reuse hidden states from the previous segment and encode position relatively rather than absolutely.
nodes.why: The first serious attack on the context-length limit, and the origin of relative position encoding.
nodes.next: Sparse attention, then RoPE and ALiBi, then the long-context race.
nodes.inherits: Relative position encoding and the idea that context length is an engineering target.

nodes.title: Language Models are Unsupervised Multitask Learners
nodes.authors: A. Radford, J. Wu, R. Child, D. Luan, D. Amodei, I. Sutskever
nodes.before: Pretrained models needed a fine-tuning stage and labelled data for each task.
nodes.problem: Could scale alone make a language model do tasks it was never trained on?
nodes.breakthrough: 1.5B parameters trained on WebText, performing translation, summarisation and QA zero-shot from prompts alone.
nodes.why: The first real evidence for the scaling hypothesis, and the origin of the staged-release norm for risky models.
nodes.next: Scaling laws formalised the trend; GPT-3 took it two orders of magnitude further.
nodes.inherits: Prompting as the interface, and byte-level BPE tokenization.

nodes.title: WebText
nodes.authors: A. Radford, J. Wu, R. Child, D. Luan, D. Amodei, I. Sutskever
nodes.before: Language models trained on curated corpora like Wikipedia and books.
nodes.problem: Curated text is small; raw web crawl is enormous but mostly junk.
nodes.breakthrough: Use human curation as a quality signal: scrape only pages linked from Reddit posts above a karma threshold.
nodes.why: It introduced proxy-based quality filtering, the ancestor of every data pipeline from C4 to FineWeb.
nodes.next: C4, the Pile, RefinedWeb and FineWeb all refined the filtering problem.
nodes.inherits: The idea that data quality filtering is a first-class part of training.

nodes.title: Generating Long Sequences with Sparse Transformers
nodes.authors: R. Child, S. Gray, A. Radford, I. Sutskever
nodes.before: Self-attention compared every position with every other, at quadratic cost.
nodes.problem: Quadratic cost makes long sequences unaffordable in both time and memory.
nodes.breakthrough: Factorise the attention pattern so each position attends to a structured subset, reducing cost to O(n sqrt n).
nodes.why: It started the sparse-attention line that runs through Longformer and BigBird to DeepSeek's sparse attention in 2025.
nodes.next: GPT-3 used these patterns; Longformer and BigBird generalised them.
nodes.inherits: Sparse attention as the standard lever for long context.

nodes.title: RoBERTa: A Robustly Optimized BERT Pretraining Approach
nodes.authors: Y. Liu, M. Ott, N. Goyal, et al. (10 authors)
nodes.before: BERT's recipe was taken as settled, and work moved to new architectures.
nodes.problem: Was BERT's ceiling architectural, or had it simply been undertrained?
nodes.breakthrough: Same architecture, more data, longer training, bigger batches, no next-sentence prediction. It beat every successor.
nodes.why: An early lesson that training recipe and data often matter more than architectural novelty.
nodes.next: The lesson resurfaces in Chinchilla and again in Llama's overtraining.
nodes.inherits: Scepticism about architecture claims that are really compute claims.

nodes.title: Sentence-BERT: Sentence Embeddings using Siamese BERT-Networks
nodes.authors: N. Reimers, I. Gurevych
nodes.before: Comparing two sentences with BERT meant running the pair through the model together.
nodes.problem: Finding the closest match in a corpus required a forward pass per candidate, which is hopeless at scale.
nodes.breakthrough: Train BERT in a siamese setup so each sentence maps to a fixed vector that can be compared with cosine similarity.
nodes.why: It turned BERT into an embedding model, which is what makes semantic search and RAG practical.
nodes.next: DPR for retrieval, and the sentence-transformers ecosystem most RAG stacks still use.
nodes.inherits: The embedding model as a separate component from the generator.

nodes.title: Megatron-LM: Training Multi-Billion Parameter Language Models Using Model Parallelism
nodes.authors: M. Shoeybi, M. Patwary, R. Puri, P. LeGresley, J. Casper, B. Catanzaro
nodes.before: Models were trained by copying the whole model onto each GPU.
nodes.problem: Past a few billion parameters, the model no longer fits on one device at all.
nodes.breakthrough: Split individual layers across GPUs with carefully placed communication, reaching 8.3B parameters on 512 GPUs.
nodes.why: The engineering that made the scaling era physically possible. Almost every large model since uses this or its descendants.
nodes.next: ZeRO complemented it; together they trained MT-NLG, PaLM and beyond.
nodes.inherits: Tensor parallelism, still part of every frontier training stack.

nodes.title: Fine-Tuning Language Models from Human Preferences
nodes.authors: D. Ziegler, N. Stiennon, J. Wu, T. Brown, A. Radford, D. Amodei, P. Christiano, G. Irving
nodes.before: Preference-based RL had been shown on robotics and games, not language.
nodes.problem: Language generation has no reward signal, and likelihood is a poor proxy for what people want.
nodes.breakthrough: Apply the reward-model-plus-RL recipe to fine-tuning a language model, on GPT-2.
nodes.why: The bridge between the 2017 RLHF idea and the assistants of 2022. Everything after is refinement and scale.
nodes.next: Summarisation from human feedback in 2020, then InstructGPT in 2022.
nodes.inherits: The three-stage pipeline: pretrain, learn a reward model, optimise the policy.

nodes.title: ZeRO: Memory Optimizations Toward Training Trillion Parameter Models
nodes.authors: S. Rajbhandari, J. Rasley, O. Ruwase, Y. He
nodes.before: Data-parallel training replicated optimizer state, gradients and weights on every GPU.
nodes.problem: That replication wastes most of the cluster's memory on identical copies.
nodes.breakthrough: Partition optimizer state, gradients and parameters across devices instead of duplicating them.
nodes.why: It removed the memory ceiling on data-parallel training and became the open-source default via DeepSpeed.
nodes.next: Used for MT-NLG, BLOOM and much of the open training ecosystem.
nodes.inherits: Sharded training state, now assumed in any large run.

nodes.title: C4: Colossal Clean Crawled Corpus
nodes.authors: C. Raffel, N. Shazeer, A. Roberts, K. Lee, S. Narang, et al. (9 authors)
nodes.before: Web-scale corpora were either proprietary or raw, unfiltered crawl.
nodes.problem: Common Crawl is mostly boilerplate, menus and noise, and nobody had published a cleaned version.
nodes.breakthrough: A documented cleaning pipeline over Common Crawl, released openly at hundreds of gigabytes.
nodes.why: The first open, reusable web corpus, which made independent replication of large pretraining possible.
nodes.next: The Pile, RefinedWeb, Dolma and FineWeb all iterate on its filtering.
nodes.inherits: The public web corpus as shared infrastructure.

nodes.title: Exploring the Limits of Transfer Learning with a Unified Text-to-Text Transformer
nodes.authors: C. Raffel, N. Shazeer, A. Roberts, K. Lee, S. Narang, et al. (9 authors)
nodes.before: Each task had its own output head, loss and evaluation convention.
nodes.problem: Incompatible task formats made it impossible to compare methods or share one model.
nodes.breakthrough: Cast every task as text in, text out, and run a controlled comparison of objectives, data and scale across them.
nodes.why: It unified the task interface, which is the conceptual step that makes instruction following possible.
nodes.next: FLAN instruction-tuned T5 models; the text-to-text framing became universal.
nodes.inherits: Everything as a text task, the assumption behind prompting.

nodes.title: BART: Denoising Sequence-to-Sequence Pre-training
nodes.authors: M. Lewis, Y. Liu, N. Goyal, et al. (8 authors)
nodes.before: BERT was good at understanding and GPT at generating, with no clean way to get both.
nodes.problem: Generation tasks needed bidirectional encoding of the input and autoregressive decoding of the output.
nodes.breakthrough: Corrupt text in several ways and train an encoder-decoder to reconstruct it.
nodes.why: It became the default seq2seq workhorse, and it is the generator inside the original RAG.
nodes.next: Used directly by RAG; the denoising family continued through T5 variants.
nodes.inherits: Encoder-decoder pretraining for conditional generation.

nodes.title: Fast Transformer Decoding: One Write-Head is All You Need
nodes.authors: N. Shazeer
nodes.before: Every attention head kept its own keys and values, all cached during generation.
nodes.problem: The KV cache dominates memory during inference and throttles throughput.
nodes.breakthrough: Share one set of keys and values across all heads, shrinking the cache dramatically.
nodes.why: The start of the inference-efficiency line that runs through GQA to DeepSeek's latent attention.
nodes.next: Grouped-query attention in 2023 found the middle ground that Llama 2 and Mistral adopted.
nodes.inherits: KV cache design, the main memory constraint when you serve a model.

nodes.title: Scaling Laws for Neural Language Models
nodes.authors: J. Kaplan, S. McCandlish, T. Henighan, et al. (10 authors)
nodes.before: Bigger models were known to be better, but nobody could say how much better in advance.
nodes.problem: Without a predictable relationship, scale-up is a gamble rather than an investment.
nodes.breakthrough: Loss falls as a smooth power law in parameters, data and compute, across seven orders of magnitude.
nodes.why: It converted scale from a hunch into a budgeting exercise, and directly motivated GPT-3.
nodes.next: GPT-3 was the demonstration; Chinchilla corrected the allocation two years later.
nodes.inherits: The practice of forecasting a model's loss before training it.

nodes.title: Dense Passage Retrieval for Open-Domain Question Answering
nodes.authors: V. Karpukhin, B. Oğuz, S. Min, P. Lewis, L. Wu, S. Edunov, D. Chen, W. Yih
nodes.before: Retrieval meant BM25 and other term-matching methods.
nodes.problem: Keyword matching misses paraphrase, so the right passage is often invisible to the retriever.
nodes.breakthrough: Two BERT encoders trained so that questions and their answering passages land near each other in vector space.
nodes.why: It beat BM25 decisively and made dense retrieval the default first stage in RAG.
nodes.next: RAG plugged it into a generator; hybrid dense-sparse retrieval followed.
nodes.inherits: The dual-encoder retriever at the front of most RAG systems.

nodes.title: Longformer: The Long-Document Transformer
nodes.authors: I. Beltagy, M. Peters, A. Cohan
nodes.before: Transformers were capped around 512 tokens by quadratic attention.
nodes.problem: Documents are longer than 512 tokens, so they had to be chunked and processed separately.
nodes.breakthrough: A sliding local window plus a few global positions, giving attention that scales linearly with length.
nodes.why: One of the first practical long-context designs, and the sliding-window pattern Mistral later revived.
nodes.next: BigBird added random attention; Mistral used sliding windows in 2023.
nodes.inherits: Windowed attention as a standard long-context tool.

nodes.title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks
nodes.authors: P. Lewis, E. Perez, A. Piktus, et al. (12 authors)
nodes.before: A model's knowledge was whatever got baked into its weights during training.
nodes.problem: Baked-in knowledge goes stale, cannot be audited, and cannot cite a source.
nodes.breakthrough: Retrieve passages with a dense retriever and condition a BART generator on them, training both together.
nodes.why: It named and popularised the pattern that most production LLM systems now use.
nodes.next: RETRO scaled retrieval to trillions of tokens; the whole vector-database industry followed.
nodes.inherits: Retrieval plus generation as the default answer to stale and unsourced knowledge.

nodes.title: Language Models are Few-Shot Learners
nodes.authors: T. Brown, B. Mann, N. Ryder, et al. (31 authors)
nodes.before: Adapting a pretrained model to a task meant gradient updates and labelled examples.
nodes.problem: Fine-tuning per task is slow, needs data, and produces a different model each time.
nodes.breakthrough: At 175B parameters, the model learns a task from examples placed in the prompt, with no weight updates at all.
nodes.why: In-context learning is the behaviour that made prompting an interface and an API business possible.
nodes.next: InstructGPT aligned it, and ChatGPT put it in front of the public.
nodes.inherits: Few-shot prompting, and the expectation that one model serves every task.

nodes.title: GShard: Scaling Giant Models with Conditional Computation
nodes.authors: D. Lepikhin, H. Lee, Y. Xu, et al. (9 authors)
nodes.before: Mixture-of-experts worked in research but was hard to distribute across accelerators.
nodes.problem: Routing tokens to experts on other devices creates communication patterns the compiler cannot infer.
nodes.breakthrough: Annotation-based sharding that lets a compiler distribute a 600B-parameter MoE automatically.
nodes.why: It made sparse models an engineering reality rather than a paper result.
nodes.next: Switch Transformer simplified the routing; Mixtral and DeepSeek inherited the approach.
nodes.inherits: Automatic sharding of expert layers across devices.

nodes.title: Big Bird: Transformers for Longer Sequences
nodes.authors: M. Zaheer, G. Guruganesh, A. Dubey, et al. (11 authors)
nodes.before: Sparse attention patterns were designed by hand with no guarantee they preserved expressiveness.
nodes.problem: Does a sparse pattern still let information flow between any two positions?
nodes.breakthrough: Global, window and random attention combined, with a proof that the result is a universal approximator of full attention.
nodes.why: It gave the sparse-attention family a theoretical footing as well as a practical one.
nodes.next: Superseded in practice by exact methods once FlashAttention made full attention cheap.
nodes.inherits: The vocabulary of global, local and random attention patterns.

nodes.title: Learning to Summarize from Human Feedback
nodes.authors: N. Stiennon, L. Ouyang, J. Wu, D. Ziegler, R. Lowe, C. Voss, A. Radford, D. Amodei, et al. (9 authors)
nodes.before: Summarisation models were trained to imitate reference summaries and scored with ROUGE.
nodes.problem: Reference summaries are not what people actually prefer, and ROUGE does not measure quality.
nodes.breakthrough: Train a reward model on human comparisons of summaries and optimise against it, beating human reference summaries.
nodes.why: The proof that RLHF works on a real language task, and the direct template for InstructGPT.
nodes.next: InstructGPT generalised the recipe from summarisation to instruction following.
nodes.inherits: The full three-stage RLHF pipeline as practised today.

nodes.title: Measuring Massive Multitask Language Understanding
nodes.authors: D. Hendrycks, C. Burns, S. Basart, A. Zou, M. Mazeika, D. Song, J. Steinhardt
nodes.before: Benchmarks like GLUE were close to saturated and measured narrow skills.
nodes.problem: No standard way to measure broad knowledge across many domains at once.
nodes.breakthrough: 57 subjects, 15,908 exam-style questions, from elementary to professional level.
nodes.why: It became the headline number in every model release for five years, for better and worse.
nodes.next: Saturated by 2024, prompting MMLU-Pro, GPQA and harder successors.
nodes.inherits: The benchmark culture that now drives model marketing.

nodes.title: An Image is Worth 16x16 Words
nodes.authors: A. Dosovitskiy, L. Beyer, A. Kolesnikov, et al. (12 authors)
nodes.before: Vision belonged to convolutional networks; transformers were for text.
nodes.problem: Two different architectures meant no shared representation between modalities.
nodes.breakthrough: Cut an image into patches, treat each as a token, and feed them to a plain Transformer encoder.
nodes.why: One architecture for pixels and words is the precondition for every multimodal model that followed.
nodes.next: CLIP, Flamingo, LLaVA and the native multimodal frontier models.
nodes.inherits: Patches as tokens, the standard way images enter an LLM.

nodes.title: The Pile: An 800GB Dataset of Diverse Text
nodes.authors: L. Gao, S. Biderman, S. Black, et al. (12 authors)
nodes.before: Frontier training data was proprietary and undocumented.
nodes.problem: Outsiders could not reproduce large-model training without a comparable corpus.
nodes.breakthrough: 825 GiB assembled from 22 documented sources, released openly.
nodes.why: It let independent groups train serious models, which is how the open ecosystem started.
nodes.next: Pythia, GPT-NeoX and OPT trained on it; later corpora refined its mix.
nodes.inherits: Open, documented pretraining data as a community resource.

nodes.title: Switch Transformers: Scaling to Trillion Parameter Models
nodes.authors: W. Fedus, B. Zoph, N. Shazeer
nodes.before: Mixture-of-experts routing sent each token to several experts, with fiddly balancing losses.
nodes.problem: Multi-expert routing was complex, unstable and communication-heavy.
nodes.breakthrough: Route each token to exactly one expert. Simpler, faster, and stable to a trillion parameters.
nodes.why: It made sparse scaling simple enough to copy, which is why MoE is now standard at the frontier.
nodes.next: Mixtral, DeepSeekMoE, Llama 4 and Kimi all descend from this simplification.
nodes.inherits: Top-1 style routing and the parameter-count-versus-active-parameters distinction.

nodes.title: Learning Transferable Visual Models From Natural Language Supervision
nodes.authors: A. Radford, J. Kim, C. Hallacy, et al. (12 authors)
nodes.before: Vision models were trained on fixed label sets like ImageNet's thousand classes.
nodes.problem: A fixed vocabulary of labels cannot describe an open world, and collecting labels does not scale.
nodes.breakthrough: Train image and text encoders contrastively on 400M web pairs so that matching pairs land together in one space.
nodes.why: It created a shared image-text space, the bridge every vision-language model crosses.
nodes.next: Flamingo, LLaVA and GPT-4V all use CLIP-style encoders.
nodes.inherits: The joint embedding space that lets a language model see.

nodes.title: RoFormer: Enhanced Transformer with Rotary Position Embedding
nodes.authors: J. Su, Y. Lu, S. Pan, A. Murtadha, B. Wen, Y. Liu
nodes.before: Position was added to embeddings, either with sinusoids or learned vectors.
nodes.problem: Added position vectors extrapolate badly past the trained length and encode distance only indirectly.
nodes.breakthrough: Rotate query and key vectors by an angle proportional to position, so attention scores depend on relative distance by construction.
nodes.why: Adopted by Llama, Mistral, Qwen, DeepSeek and most others. It is the position encoding of the current era.
nodes.next: Position interpolation and YaRN extend RoPE to longer contexts.
nodes.inherits: Relative position through rotation, in nearly every open model you will run.

nodes.title: LoRA: Low-Rank Adaptation of Large Language Models
nodes.authors: E. Hu, Y. Shen, P. Wallis, et al. (8 authors)
nodes.before: Fine-tuning updated every weight and produced a full-size copy per task.
nodes.problem: A 175B model cannot be fine-tuned, stored or served per task by most organisations.
nodes.breakthrough: Freeze the base model and train a small low-rank update alongside it, often under 1% of parameters.
nodes.why: It turned fine-tuning from a datacentre operation into something you can do on one GPU.
nodes.next: QLoRA added quantization; adapters became the standard customisation route.
nodes.inherits: Parameter-efficient fine-tuning, the default way people specialise open models.

nodes.title: GitHub Copilot
nodes.authors: GitHub
nodes.before: Code completion used static analysis of the current file and project.
nodes.problem: Nobody had shipped a large language model into a daily professional workflow.
nodes.breakthrough: Codex behind an editor plugin, suggesting whole functions from a comment or signature.
nodes.why: The first mass-market LLM product, eighteen months before ChatGPT, and the start of AI coding as a category.
nodes.next: Chat interfaces, then agentic coding tools that edit repositories directly.
nodes.inherits: AI assistance as a normal part of writing software.

nodes.title: Evaluating Large Language Models Trained on Code
nodes.authors: M. Chen, J. Tworek, H. Jun, et al. (58 authors)
nodes.before: Code generation was evaluated by text similarity to a reference solution.
nodes.problem: Similarity to a reference says nothing about whether the code runs correctly.
nodes.breakthrough: Fine-tune GPT on public code and evaluate by executing unit tests, via the HumanEval benchmark.
nodes.why: Functional correctness as the metric is why coding became the field's clearest measure of progress.
nodes.next: Copilot productised it; HumanEval led to SWE-bench and the agentic coding benchmarks.
nodes.inherits: Execution-based evaluation, now standard for code models.

nodes.title: Train Short, Test Long: Attention with Linear Biases
nodes.authors: O. Press, N. Smith, M. Lewis
nodes.before: Models trained at one context length degraded sharply when run on longer inputs.
nodes.problem: Position embeddings do not generalise past the lengths they were trained on.
nodes.breakthrough: Drop position embeddings and instead subtract a penalty from attention scores proportional to distance.
nodes.why: It framed length extrapolation as a goal in itself and offered the main alternative to RoPE.
nodes.next: Used in BLOOM; RoPE with interpolation eventually won more adopters.
nodes.inherits: Length extrapolation as an explicit design criterion.

nodes.title: Finetuned Language Models Are Zero-Shot Learners
nodes.authors: J. Wei, M. Bosma, V. Zhao, K. Guu, A. Yu, B. Lester, N. Du, A. Dai, et al. (9 authors)
nodes.before: Few-shot prompting worked, but models did not reliably follow a plain instruction.
nodes.problem: A pretrained model completes text; it has no particular reason to do what you ask.
nodes.breakthrough: Fine-tune on many tasks phrased as natural-language instructions, then test on held-out task types.
nodes.why: Instruction following turned out to be a learnable skill that generalises. This is the step before RLHF.
nodes.next: T0 in parallel, Flan-T5 at scale, and InstructGPT's supervised stage.
nodes.inherits: Instruction tuning as the first stage of every assistant's post-training.

nodes.title: Multitask Prompted Training Enables Zero-Shot Task Generalization
nodes.authors: V. Sanh, A. Webson, C. Raffel, et al. (~40 authors)
nodes.before: Instruction tuning was being explored inside large industrial labs.
nodes.problem: Nobody outside those labs had the prompts, the data or the models to study it.
nodes.breakthrough: An open collection of prompt templates across tasks, plus openly released instruction-tuned models.
nodes.why: It made instruction tuning reproducible in the open, months before ChatGPT made it famous.
nodes.next: The prompt collections fed the Flan collection and later open instruction datasets.
nodes.inherits: Open instruction data as shared infrastructure.

nodes.title: A General Language Assistant as a Laboratory for Alignment
nodes.authors: A. Askell, Y. Bai, A. Chen, et al. (22 authors)
nodes.before: Alignment was discussed abstractly or studied on narrow tasks.
nodes.problem: No concrete definition of what a well-behaved general assistant should optimise for.
nodes.breakthrough: Frame the target as helpful, honest and harmless, and use a general assistant as the testbed for alignment methods.
nodes.why: The HHH framing organised Anthropic's work and much of the field's vocabulary for assistant behaviour.
nodes.next: The HH-RLHF paper and Constitutional AI build directly on it.
nodes.inherits: Helpful, honest, harmless as the shorthand for assistant objectives.

nodes.title: Scaling Language Models: Methods, Analysis and Insights from Training Gopher
nodes.authors: J. Rae, S. Borgeaud, T. Cai, et al. (80 authors)
nodes.before: GPT-3 was the reference point, with limited public analysis of what scale does.
nodes.problem: Which capabilities improve with scale, and which do not?
nodes.breakthrough: A 280B model evaluated across 152 tasks, showing gains concentrated in knowledge tasks and much weaker in reasoning.
nodes.why: It supplied the careful evaluation that scaling claims lacked, and the compute budget Chinchilla reanalysed.
nodes.next: Chinchilla used the same budget to show Gopher was badly undertrained.
nodes.inherits: The habit of broad, task-by-task evaluation of scale.

nodes.title: Improving Language Models by Retrieving from Trillions of Tokens
nodes.authors: S. Borgeaud, A. Mensch, J. Hoffmann, et al. (28 authors)
nodes.before: Retrieval was bolted on at inference time to a model trained without it.
nodes.problem: If a model can look things up, it should not have to memorise them in its weights.
nodes.breakthrough: Retrieve from a two-trillion-token database during pretraining itself, via chunked cross-attention.
nodes.why: It showed a 7B model with retrieval matching much larger ones, arguing memory and reasoning can be separated.
nodes.next: The idea recurs in long-context and memory work, though frontier labs largely chose bigger contexts instead.
nodes.inherits: The open question of what belongs in weights versus in an external store.

nodes.title: WebGPT: Browser-assisted question-answering with human feedback
nodes.authors: R. Nakano, J. Hilton, S. Balaji, et al. (18 authors)
nodes.before: Models answered from their weights alone, with no way to check anything.
nodes.problem: Long-form answers were unsourced and often confidently wrong.
nodes.breakthrough: Give the model a text browser, train it with human feedback to search, navigate and cite, then answer.
nodes.why: The first real tool-using language model, and the ancestor of every research and browsing agent.
nodes.next: ReAct formalised the loop; Toolformer learned tool calls without demonstrations.
nodes.inherits: The model that acts in an environment rather than only emitting text.

nodes.title: LaMDA: Language Models for Dialog Applications
nodes.authors: R. Thoppilan, D. De Freitas, J. Hall, et al. (~60 authors)
nodes.before: Large models were tuned for completion, not for holding a conversation.
nodes.problem: Dialogue needs safety, factual grounding and a consistent persona, none of which come free.
nodes.breakthrough: Dialogue-specific fine-tuning with safety and groundedness objectives, plus external tool lookups for facts.
nodes.why: Google had an aligned conversational model well before ChatGPT and chose not to ship it publicly.
nodes.next: Bard in 2023, then the Gemini line.
nodes.inherits: Safety and groundedness as explicit fine-tuning targets for chat.

nodes.title: Chain-of-Thought Prompting Elicits Reasoning in Large Language Models
nodes.authors: J. Wei, X. Wang, D. Schuurmans, et al. (9 authors)
nodes.before: Models answered arithmetic and logic questions in one step and got them wrong.
nodes.problem: Hard problems need intermediate work, but nothing in the prompt asked for it.
nodes.breakthrough: Put worked examples showing the reasoning steps in the prompt, and the model reasons step by step too.
nodes.why: It showed reasoning was latent and could be elicited, which is the seed of the entire test-time compute era.
nodes.next: Zero-shot CoT, self-consistency, tree of thoughts, and eventually RL-trained reasoning in o1 and R1.
nodes.inherits: Thinking before answering, now trained in rather than prompted for.

nodes.title: Megatron-Turing NLG 530B
nodes.authors: S. Smith, M. Patwary, B. Norick, et al. (20 authors)
nodes.before: GPT-3's 175B was the largest dense model publicly described.
nodes.problem: Could dense training be pushed further, and what does it take in engineering terms?
nodes.breakthrough: 530B dense parameters trained with combined tensor, pipeline and data parallelism.
nodes.why: The high-water mark of pure dense scaling, and the clearest evidence that this path was hitting diminishing returns.
nodes.next: Chinchilla redirected the field toward data; sparsity took the parameter-count crown.
nodes.inherits: Mostly a cautionary datapoint about scaling parameters without scaling data.

nodes.title: Competition-Level Code Generation with AlphaCode
nodes.authors: Y. Li, D. Choi, J. Chung, et al. (26 authors)
nodes.before: Code models produced one attempt per problem.
nodes.problem: Competitive programming problems are too hard to solve first try.
nodes.breakthrough: Generate a million candidate programs, filter by running the examples, and cluster to pick submissions.
nodes.why: An early argument that spending more compute at inference buys accuracy, which is the test-time compute thesis.
nodes.next: Self-consistency, verifier-guided search and eventually reasoning models.
nodes.inherits: Sampling widely and filtering, rather than trusting a single generation.

nodes.title: Training language models to follow instructions with human feedback
nodes.authors: L. Ouyang, J. Wu, X. Jiang, et al. (20 authors)
nodes.before: GPT-3 was capable but continued your text instead of doing what you asked.
nodes.problem: Likelihood on web text is not the same objective as being useful to a person.
nodes.breakthrough: Supervised fine-tuning on demonstrations, then a reward model from human rankings, then PPO against it.
nodes.why: A 1.3B InstructGPT was preferred to the 175B base model. Alignment elicits and steers capability rather than adding knowledge.
nodes.next: ChatGPT shipped this recipe to the public eight months later.
nodes.inherits: The post-training stack every assistant uses.

nodes.title: Self-Consistency Improves Chain of Thought Reasoning
nodes.authors: X. Wang, J. Wei, D. Schuurmans, Q. Le, E. Chi, S. Narang, A. Chowdhery, D. Zhou
nodes.before: Chain of thought produced one reasoning path, decoded greedily.
nodes.problem: A single path fails if any step goes wrong, and greedy decoding is arbitrary.
nodes.breakthrough: Sample many reasoning paths and take the most common final answer.
nodes.why: The cleanest demonstration that extra inference compute converts directly into accuracy.
nodes.next: Tree of thoughts, verifier-guided search, and the reasoning models of 2024.
nodes.inherits: Majority voting over samples, still a standard evaluation trick.

nodes.title: STaR: Bootstrapping Reasoning With Reasoning
nodes.authors: E. Zelikman, Y. Wu, J. Mu, N. Goodman
nodes.before: Reasoning was prompted at inference; training on reasoning needed human-written rationales.
nodes.problem: Nobody can write rationales for every problem a model should learn to solve.
nodes.breakthrough: Let the model generate its own rationales, keep the ones that reach the right answer, and fine-tune on those.
nodes.why: Self-generated reasoning data, verified by outcome, is the core loop that RL-trained reasoning models later industrialised.
nodes.next: Process supervision, then the RL reasoning training in o1 and DeepSeek-R1.
nodes.inherits: Training on a model's own verified reasoning.

nodes.title: Training Compute-Optimal Large Language Models
nodes.authors: J. Hoffmann, S. Borgeaud, A. Mensch, et al. (22 authors)
nodes.before: Scaling laws were read as licence to grow parameters faster than data.
nodes.problem: Everyone's models were far too large for the number of tokens they saw.
nodes.breakthrough: Over 400 training runs showing parameters and data should scale together, roughly 20 tokens per parameter. A 70B model beat the 280B Gopher.
nodes.why: It redirected the field from parameter count toward data, which is why capable small models exist at all.
nodes.next: Llama took it further, overtraining small models for cheap inference.
nodes.inherits: Compute allocation as a design decision, not an afterthought.

nodes.title: PaLM: Scaling Language Modeling with Pathways
nodes.authors: A. Chowdhery, S. Narang, J. Devlin, et al. (67 authors)
nodes.before: Reasoning gains from scale looked modest and uneven.
nodes.problem: Would more scale actually help on tasks requiring multi-step inference?
nodes.breakthrough: 540B dense parameters trained across TPU pods, reaching breakthrough results on reasoning benchmarks with chain-of-thought prompting.
nodes.why: It supplied the strongest evidence for the scale-unlocks-reasoning story, and the discontinuities that fed the emergence debate.
nodes.next: Flan-PaLM instruction-tuned it; Gemini succeeded it.
nodes.inherits: The pairing of large scale with chain-of-thought as the reasoning recipe of 2022.

nodes.title: Training a Helpful and Harmless Assistant with RLHF
nodes.authors: Y. Bai, A. Jones, K. Ndousse, et al. (31 authors)
nodes.before: RLHF results came from one lab, with private data.
nodes.problem: Helpfulness and harmlessness pull against each other, and nobody had studied the tradeoff openly.
nodes.breakthrough: A full RLHF assistant study separating the two objectives, with the human preference dataset released.
nodes.why: It gave the open community real preference data and named the tension every assistant has to manage.
nodes.next: Constitutional AI replaced much of the human harmlessness labelling with AI feedback.
nodes.inherits: The helpfulness-harmlessness tradeoff, and open preference datasets.

nodes.title: Flamingo: a Visual Language Model for Few-Shot Learning
nodes.authors: J. Alayrac, J. Donahue, P. Luc, et al. (27 authors)
nodes.before: Vision-language models were trained end to end for specific tasks like captioning.
nodes.problem: Retraining a language model for vision throws away its language ability and costs a fortune.
nodes.breakthrough: Freeze a pretrained vision encoder and a pretrained language model, and train only cross-attention layers to bridge them.
nodes.why: The bridging recipe that made multimodality affordable, and the template LLaVA and others followed.
nodes.next: LLaVA did it cheaply and openly; GPT-4V and Gemini made it a product.
nodes.inherits: Bolting vision onto a language model by training an adapter between frozen parts.

nodes.title: OPT: Open Pre-trained Transformer Language Models
nodes.authors: S. Zhang, S. Roller, N. Goyal, et al. (19 authors)
nodes.before: GPT-3-scale models existed only behind APIs, with no access to weights.
nodes.problem: You cannot study a model's internals, biases or failure modes through an API.
nodes.breakthrough: A 175B model released to researchers, with the full training logbook including the failures.
nodes.why: The first at-scale open replication, and the logbook taught the community what large training runs actually feel like.
nodes.next: BLOOM, then LLaMA, then the open ecosystem proper.
nodes.inherits: The norm of releasing weights and documenting the process.

nodes.title: Large Language Models are Zero-Shot Reasoners
nodes.authors: T. Kojima, S. Gu, M. Reid, Y. Matsuo, Y. Iwasawa
nodes.before: Chain of thought needed hand-written worked examples in the prompt.
nodes.problem: Writing exemplars for every task is laborious and task-specific.
nodes.breakthrough: A single phrase asking the model to think step by step, with no examples, unlocks most of the same gain.
nodes.why: It showed the reasoning behaviour was already in the model, waiting for a cue. Cheap, universal, and much copied.
nodes.next: Absorbed into system prompts everywhere, then trained in directly by reasoning models.
nodes.inherits: The instruction to reason before answering.

nodes.title: FlashAttention: Fast and Memory-Efficient Exact Attention with IO-Awareness
nodes.authors: T. Dao, D. Fu, S. Ermon, A. Rudra, C. Ré
nodes.before: Long context was attacked by approximating attention with sparse patterns.
nodes.problem: Attention was slow because of memory traffic between GPU levels, not because of arithmetic.
nodes.breakthrough: Tile the computation so it stays in fast on-chip memory and never writes the full attention matrix. Exact, not approximate.
nodes.why: It made long context an engineering problem rather than an architectural compromise, and most approximations became unnecessary.
nodes.next: FlashAttention-2 and 3, vLLM's serving stack, and the long-context race.
nodes.inherits: The kernel your model is almost certainly using right now.

nodes.title: Emergent Abilities of Large Language Models
nodes.authors: J. Wei, Y. Tay, R. Bommasani, et al. (16 authors)
nodes.before: Scaling laws described smooth, predictable improvement in loss.
nodes.problem: Some abilities appeared absent at small scale and present at large scale, which smooth curves do not explain.
nodes.breakthrough: A catalogue of tasks where performance jumps sharply past a scale threshold, framed as emergence.
nodes.why: It shaped how the field talked about capability and risk for two years, and provoked a serious rebuttal in 2023.
nodes.next: Schaeffer's mirage paper argued the jumps come from discontinuous metrics, not the models.
nodes.inherits: An unresolved argument about whether capability arrives smoothly or in steps.

nodes.title: BLOOM: A 176B-Parameter Open-Access Multilingual Language Model
nodes.authors: BigScience (Scao et al., 1000+ contributors)
nodes.before: Large models were built inside single companies and released, if at all, on their terms.
nodes.problem: No model of that scale had been built by an open scientific collaboration, and none covered many languages well.
nodes.breakthrough: A 176B multilingual model trained in public by a thousand researchers on a national supercomputer, released with a responsible-use licence.
nodes.why: It proved a large model could be built as open science, and put multilingual coverage on the agenda.
nodes.next: The RAIL licence influenced later custom licences; the collaboration model informed open data efforts.
nodes.inherits: Open collaborative training, and the idea of use-restricted rather than fully free licences.

nodes.title: LLM.int8(): 8-bit Matrix Multiplication for Transformers at Scale
nodes.authors: T. Dettmers, M. Lewis, Y. Belkada, L. Zettlemoyer
nodes.inst: U. Washington / Meta AI / Hugging Face
nodes.before: Running a 175B model meant a multi-GPU server holding 16-bit weights.
nodes.problem: Naive 8-bit quantization destroyed accuracy because of rare outlier features.
nodes.breakthrough: Quantize almost everything to 8-bit while keeping outlier dimensions in 16-bit, with no measured degradation.
nodes.why: It halved the memory needed to run big models and started the quantization toolchain most local inference uses.
nodes.next: GPTQ and AWQ pushed to 4-bit; QLoRA made 4-bit trainable.
nodes.inherits: Quantized inference as the normal way to run a model you did not train.

nodes.title: Robust Speech Recognition via Large-Scale Weak Supervision
nodes.authors: A. Radford, J. Kim, T. Xu, G. Brockman, C. McLeavey, I. Sutskever
nodes.before: Speech recognition models were trained on small curated corpora and fine-tuned per domain.
nodes.problem: They broke on accents, noise and languages outside their training set.
nodes.breakthrough: 680,000 hours of weakly supervised multilingual audio, trained as a single sequence-to-sequence model.
nodes.why: It made robust open speech recognition a commodity, which is the input side of every voice assistant built since.
nodes.next: Voice interfaces on top of LLMs, then natively audio-capable models like GPT-4o.
nodes.inherits: Speech as just another sequence task for a transformer.

nodes.title: ReAct: Synergizing Reasoning and Acting in Language Models
nodes.authors: S. Yao, J. Zhao, D. Yu, N. Du, I. Shafran, K. Narasimhan, Y. Cao
nodes.before: Reasoning and tool use were separate lines: chain-of-thought thought, WebGPT acted.
nodes.problem: Pure reasoning hallucinates facts; pure acting has no plan.
nodes.breakthrough: Interleave them in one loop: a thought, an action, an observation, repeat.
nodes.why: This loop is the skeleton of essentially every agent framework that followed.
nodes.next: Reflexion added memory, Toolformer learned the calls, and coding agents industrialised it.
nodes.inherits: The thought-action-observation cycle at the heart of agents.

nodes.title: Scaling Instruction-Finetuned Language Models
nodes.authors: H. Chung, L. Hou, S. Longpre, et al. (35 authors)
nodes.before: Instruction tuning had been shown on dozens of tasks at moderate scale.
nodes.problem: Did it keep working with more tasks, bigger models and reasoning data mixed in?
nodes.breakthrough: Scale to 1,800 tasks and add chain-of-thought examples to the instruction mixture.
nodes.why: It made instruction tuning a scalable recipe, and the released Flan-T5 models became a research workhorse.
nodes.next: The Flan collection fed open instruction datasets; the recipe is standard post-training practice.
nodes.inherits: Instruction mixtures that include reasoning traces.

nodes.title: GPTQ: Accurate Post-Training Quantization for Generative Pre-trained Transformers
nodes.authors: E. Frantar, S. Ashkboos, T. Hoefler, D. Alistarh
nodes.before: 8-bit quantization worked; 4-bit lost too much accuracy to be usable.
nodes.problem: Even 8-bit weights leave the largest models out of reach of a single GPU.
nodes.breakthrough: One-shot second-order weight rounding that holds accuracy at 3 to 4 bits, in a few GPU hours.
nodes.why: 4-bit is what makes a 70B model fit on consumer hardware. This is why local inference is possible at all.
nodes.next: AWQ traded a different accuracy-speed point; GGUF packaged quantized weights for llama.cpp.
nodes.inherits: The 4-bit quantized checkpoint as the standard local format.

nodes.title: ChatGPT
nodes.authors: OpenAI
nodes.before: Aligned instruction-following models existed, reachable through a developer API.
nodes.problem: Nobody outside the industry had a reason or a way to use one.
nodes.breakthrough: The same RLHF technique in a free chat box, with dialogue-formatted training data and a conversational memory.
nodes.why: No new capability, and the biggest inflection in the field's history. It was a distribution and interface breakthrough.
nodes.next: GPT-4 and Claude followed as products; every lab reorganised around assistants.
nodes.inherits: Chat as the default interface to a language model.

nodes.title: GPT-3.5 series
nodes.authors: OpenAI
nodes.before: GPT-3 was the deployed base model, with InstructGPT as a research result.
nodes.problem: The research recipe had to become a maintained product line.
nodes.breakthrough: A family of instruction-tuned GPT-3 descendants, including the code-trained variants, serving the API and ChatGPT.
nodes.why: The model behind ChatGPT's launch, and the one whose outputs trained Alpaca and much of the early open ecosystem.
nodes.next: GPT-4 replaced it at the frontier; distillation from it seeded open instruction models.
nodes.inherits: The production instruction-tuned model as a distinct artefact from the base model.

nodes.title: Fast Inference from Transformers via Speculative Decoding
nodes.other: ICML 2023; Chen et al. 2023 in parallel
nodes.authors: Y. Leviathan, M. Kalman, Y. Matias
nodes.before: Generation produced one token per forward pass, however small the next token's uncertainty.
nodes.problem: Decoding is memory-bound and serial, so most of the GPU sits idle.
nodes.breakthrough: A small draft model proposes several tokens, the large model verifies them in one pass, and rejected tokens are corrected. Output is identical.
nodes.why: Two to three times faster generation with no quality loss, now standard in serving stacks.
nodes.next: Built into vLLM and most inference engines; the idea recurs in later decoding work.
nodes.inherits: Draft-and-verify decoding in the systems that serve your requests.

nodes.title: Constitutional AI: Harmlessness from AI Feedback
nodes.authors: Y. Bai, S. Kadavath, S. Kundu, et al.
nodes.before: Harmlessness came from humans labelling large volumes of unpleasant model output.
nodes.problem: That labour is expensive, distressing, and its criteria live in labellers' heads rather than on paper.
nodes.breakthrough: Write the principles down, have the model critique and revise its own outputs against them, and train on its own feedback.
nodes.why: It moved part of alignment from tacit labelling to explicit written rules, and made the criteria auditable.
nodes.next: RLAIF more broadly, and the alignment approach behind Claude.
nodes.inherits: AI feedback against stated principles as a supplement to human preference data.

nodes.title: Self-Instruct: Aligning Language Models with Self-Generated Instructions
nodes.authors: Y. Wang, Y. Kordi, S. Mishra, A. Liu, N. Smith, D. Khashabi, H. Hajishirzi
nodes.before: Instruction tuning needed human-written instruction-response pairs.
nodes.problem: Writing tens of thousands of examples by hand is slow and expensive.
nodes.breakthrough: Bootstrap from a small seed set: have the model write new instructions and answers, filter, and train on the result.
nodes.why: It made instruction data nearly free, which is how small open models caught up so quickly in 2023.
nodes.next: Alpaca applied it to GPT-3.5 outputs; the synthetic data line runs on to phi and beyond.
nodes.inherits: Synthetic instruction data as a normal ingredient.

nodes.title: Toolformer: Language Models Can Teach Themselves to Use Tools
nodes.authors: T. Schick, J. Dwivedi-Yu, R. Dessì, et al. (8 authors)
nodes.before: Tool use was taught with human demonstrations or elaborate prompting.
nodes.problem: Demonstrations are expensive and do not transfer to new tools.
nodes.breakthrough: Let the model insert candidate API calls into text, keep the ones that reduce its own loss, and fine-tune on those.
nodes.why: It framed tool use as something a model can learn by itself from its own uncertainty.
nodes.next: Function calling APIs made tool use a product feature months later.
nodes.inherits: Tool calls as tokens the model emits, rather than an external orchestration layer.

nodes.title: LLaMA: Open and Efficient Foundation Language Models
nodes.authors: H. Touvron, T. Lavril, G. Izacard, et al. (14 authors)
nodes.before: Open models were either small or, like OPT and BLOOM, expensive to run and behind the frontier.
nodes.problem: Nobody had released a model that was both genuinely good and small enough to be useful on modest hardware.
nodes.breakthrough: Train smaller models far past compute-optimal on public data alone. LLaMA-13B outperformed GPT-3 175B.
nodes.why: The single most consequential open release. Everything in the 2023 open ecosystem is downstream of these weights.
nodes.next: Alpaca, llama.cpp, QLoRA and Llama 2 within months.
nodes.inherits: The small-but-overtrained recipe every open model now follows.

nodes.title: llama.cpp
nodes.authors: Georgi Gerganov and contributors
nodes.before: Running a model meant Python, CUDA and a datacentre GPU.
nodes.problem: Most people have a laptop, not an A100.
nodes.breakthrough: A dependency-free C++ inference engine with quantized weights, running LLaMA on a CPU or a MacBook.
nodes.why: It created local inference as a mass activity, and GGUF became the format the whole local ecosystem shares.
nodes.next: Ollama and the local-model tooling built on top of it.
nodes.inherits: The assumption that you can run a capable model on your own machine.

nodes.title: Stanford Alpaca
nodes.authors: R. Taori, I. Gulrajani, T. Zhang, et al.
nodes.before: Instruction tuning was assumed to need industrial resources and proprietary data.
nodes.problem: Could a university group turn a base model into an assistant for pocket change?
nodes.breakthrough: 52,000 self-instruct examples generated from text-davinci-003, used to fine-tune LLaMA 7B for a few hundred dollars.
nodes.why: It showed capability could be distilled cheaply from a stronger model, which set off the open fine-tune explosion and the licensing fights.
nodes.next: Vicuna and dozens of derivatives; distillation became standard practice and a terms-of-service problem.
nodes.inherits: Cheap instruction tuning by distilling from a stronger model.

nodes.title: Claude
nodes.authors: Anthropic
nodes.before: ChatGPT had the assistant market to itself.
nodes.problem: Was constitutional training a viable basis for a competitive commercial assistant?
nodes.breakthrough: An assistant aligned with Constitutional AI rather than primarily human harmlessness labelling.
nodes.why: It established a second frontier lab with a distinct alignment method, and a competitive market for assistants.
nodes.next: The Claude 2, 3, 4 and 5 generations, and the long-context and agentic coding lines.
nodes.inherits: A plural frontier rather than a single provider.

nodes.title: GPT-4 Technical Report
nodes.authors: OpenAI
nodes.before: GPT-3.5 was the deployed frontier, text only, and error-prone on hard reasoning.
nodes.problem: How far could the recipe be pushed, and could performance be predicted before training?
nodes.breakthrough: A large capability jump with image input, and infrastructure that predicted final performance from small-scale runs.
nodes.why: It set the bar every other lab measured against for over a year, and its outputs trained much of the open ecosystem.
nodes.next: GPT-4V added vision publicly, GPT-4 Turbo added context, then GPT-4o unified modalities.
nodes.inherits: Predictable scaling as an engineering discipline, and multimodal input as standard.

nodes.title: Reflexion: Language Agents with Verbal Reinforcement Learning
nodes.authors: N. Shinn, F. Cassano, E. Berman, A. Gopinath, K. Narasimhan, S. Yao
nodes.before: An agent that failed a task simply failed and started over.
nodes.problem: Improving from failure normally means gradient updates, which is impossible at inference time.
nodes.breakthrough: Have the agent write a verbal post-mortem of its failure and keep it in memory for the next attempt.
nodes.why: Learning from experience without touching the weights, which became a standard pattern in agent design.
nodes.next: Memory and self-critique layers in agent frameworks and coding agents.
nodes.inherits: Episodic self-reflection as an agent's cheap substitute for training.

nodes.title: AutoGPT
nodes.authors: Significant-Gravitas (Toran Bruce Richards)
nodes.before: Agent loops were research prototypes described in papers.
nodes.problem: Nobody had packaged one so that an ordinary developer could run it against a goal.
nodes.breakthrough: An open loop that plans, calls tools, writes files and recurses until a goal is met, using GPT-4.
nodes.why: It made autonomous agents a mainstream idea, and its unreliability taught the field what was actually hard.
nodes.next: The sober descendants are today's coding agents with tight scopes and verification.
nodes.inherits: Public expectations about agents, both the enthusiasm and the scepticism.

nodes.title: Pythia: A Suite for Analyzing Large Language Models Across Training and Scaling
nodes.authors: S. Biderman, H. Schoelkopf, Q. Anthony, et al. (13 authors)
nodes.before: Open models were released as final checkpoints with no training history.
nodes.problem: You cannot study how capabilities emerge if you only see the finished model.
nodes.breakthrough: Sixteen models across scales, trained on identical data in identical order, with 154 checkpoints each released.
nodes.why: It turned training dynamics into something outsiders could actually study, including memorisation and bias formation.
nodes.next: OLMo extended the fully-open approach to frontier-adjacent scale.
nodes.inherits: Open checkpoints and data order as research infrastructure.

nodes.title: Visual Instruction Tuning
nodes.authors: H. Liu, C. Li, Q. Wu, Y. Lee
nodes.before: Vision-language models came from large labs with large budgets.
nodes.problem: There was no open recipe for giving an open language model eyes.
nodes.breakthrough: A simple projection layer between CLIP and an open LLM, trained on visual instruction data generated by GPT-4.
nodes.why: It made open multimodal models buildable in a day, and set the template most open VLMs still use.
nodes.next: A wave of open vision-language models, and the multimodal expectations that followed.
nodes.inherits: The projector-between-encoder-and-LLM design.

nodes.title: Are Emergent Abilities of Large Language Models a Mirage?
nodes.authors: R. Schaeffer, B. Miranda, S. Koyejo
nodes.before: Sudden capability jumps with scale were widely accepted and used in safety arguments.
nodes.problem: The jumps were measured with all-or-nothing metrics like exact match.
nodes.breakthrough: Show that the same runs look smooth under continuous metrics, so the discontinuity may be in the ruler, not the model.
nodes.why: A rare, effective correction to a dominant narrative, and a caution about how capability claims are measured.
nodes.next: More careful evaluation methodology, and continuing disagreement about what emergence means.
nodes.inherits: Scepticism about benchmark discontinuities as evidence.

nodes.title: 100K context windows
nodes.authors: Anthropic
nodes.before: Production context windows were 4K to 8K tokens, occasionally 32K.
nodes.problem: Anything book-length had to be chunked and retrieved rather than read.
nodes.breakthrough: A deployed 100,000-token window, enough for a novel or a large codebase in one prompt.
nodes.why: It opened the long-context era in products and began the running argument about retrieval versus a bigger window.
nodes.next: Gemini 1.5's million tokens, and the long-context race through 2026.
nodes.inherits: The expectation that a model can read a whole document.

nodes.title: Tree of Thoughts: Deliberate Problem Solving with Large Language Models
nodes.authors: S. Yao, D. Yu, J. Zhao, I. Shafran, T. Griffiths, Y. Cao, K. Narasimhan
nodes.before: Reasoning ran forward in a single line, or in several independent lines aggregated by vote.
nodes.problem: Some problems need exploring alternatives, evaluating them, and backtracking.
nodes.breakthrough: Treat reasoning steps as nodes in a tree, with the model proposing and scoring branches, plus search over them.
nodes.why: It brought classical search into language-model reasoning, the conceptual bridge to test-time compute.
nodes.next: Verifier-guided search, process supervision, and the RL reasoning models.
nodes.inherits: Search over reasoning as a way to spend inference compute.

nodes.title: GQA: Training Generalized Multi-Query Transformer Models
nodes.authors: J. Ainslie, J. Lee-Thorp, M. de Jong, Y. Zemlyanskiy, F. Lebrón, S. Sanghai
nodes.before: You chose between multi-head attention, which was accurate but memory-hungry, and multi-query, which was fast but lossy.
nodes.problem: Multi-query attention degraded quality; multi-head attention throttled inference.
nodes.breakthrough: Share keys and values across small groups of heads, and convert existing checkpoints cheaply.
nodes.why: Llama 2, Mistral, Qwen and most models since use it. It is the default attention layout today.
nodes.next: DeepSeek's latent attention pushed the same goal further.
nodes.inherits: The attention variant in almost every model you will run.

nodes.title: QLoRA: Efficient Finetuning of Quantized LLMs
nodes.authors: T. Dettmers, A. Pagnoni, A. Holtzman, L. Zettlemoyer
nodes.before: LoRA made fine-tuning cheap, but the frozen base model still had to fit in memory at 16-bit.
nodes.problem: A 65B base model needs hundreds of gigabytes, so the adapters did not help enough.
nodes.breakthrough: Quantize the frozen base to 4-bit with a data-type suited to normal weights, and backpropagate through it into the adapters. 65B on one 48GB GPU.
nodes.why: It put fine-tuning of large models within reach of individuals, and the resulting models were competitive.
