nodes.next: The open fine-tuning ecosystem as it exists now.
nodes.inherits: Quantized base plus small trainable adapters, the standard cheap fine-tune.

nodes.title: Falcon / RefinedWeb models
nodes.authors: TII (Almazrouei et al.)
nodes.before: The best open weights carried non-commercial licences.
nodes.problem: Businesses could not build on LLaMA, and the alternatives were weaker.
nodes.breakthrough: A competitive 40B model trained on filtered web data, relicensed to Apache 2.0 within a week of release.
nodes.why: It briefly led the open leaderboards and proved permissive licensing at scale was possible before Llama 2 followed.
nodes.next: Llama 2's commercial licence, then Mistral's Apache releases.
nodes.inherits: Permissive licensing as a competitive lever.

nodes.title: Direct Preference Optimization
nodes.authors: R. Rafailov, A. Sharma, E. Mitchell, S. Ermon, C. Manning, C. Finn
nodes.before: Preference alignment meant training a reward model then running PPO against it.
nodes.problem: That pipeline is unstable, memory-hungry and hard to reproduce outside well-resourced labs.
nodes.breakthrough: Algebra showing the RL objective can be optimised directly on preference pairs, with no reward model and no RL loop.
nodes.why: It made alignment a straightforward fine-tuning job, which is why open models could align themselves at all.
nodes.next: Adopted in Llama 3's post-training and across the open ecosystem.
nodes.inherits: Preference optimisation as a simple loss rather than an RL system.

nodes.title: Let's Verify Step by Step
nodes.authors: H. Lightman, V. Kosaraju, Y. Burda, et al. (10 authors)
nodes.before: Reasoning was rewarded by whether the final answer was right.
nodes.problem: A model can reach the right answer through faulty reasoning, and outcome rewards teach it to keep doing that.
nodes.breakthrough: Reward each reasoning step individually, with 800,000 human step-level labels released.
nodes.why: Process supervision beat outcome supervision decisively, and is a visible ancestor of the RL-trained reasoning models.
nodes.next: Reward models over reasoning steps, then o1 and DeepSeek-R1.
nodes.inherits: Judging the reasoning, not only the answer.

nodes.title: AWQ: Activation-aware Weight Quantization
nodes.authors: J. Lin, J. Tang, H. Tang, et al. (10 authors)
nodes.before: 4-bit quantization decided which weights to protect using the weights themselves.
nodes.problem: Weight magnitude is the wrong signal; what matters is which weights see large activations.
nodes.breakthrough: Use activation statistics to choose the salient channels to preserve, with no backpropagation needed.
nodes.why: Better accuracy at 4-bit and faster kernels, and one of the two quantization formats local tooling offers.
nodes.next: Standard in vLLM and local inference alongside GPTQ and GGUF.
nodes.inherits: Activation-aware quantization in the serving stack.

nodes.title: The RefinedWeb Dataset for Falcon LLM
nodes.authors: G. Penedo, Q. Malartic, D. Hesslow, et al. (9 authors)
nodes.before: Best practice mixed filtered web text with curated sources like books and Wikipedia.
nodes.problem: Curated corpora are small and legally awkward; is the curation actually necessary?
nodes.breakthrough: Aggressive filtering and deduplication of web data alone, matching or beating models trained on curated mixes.
nodes.why: It reframed data quality as a filtering problem rather than a sourcing problem, which is how the field now treats it.
nodes.next: Dolma and FineWeb refined the same pipeline in the open.
nodes.inherits: Web-only pretraining data with heavy filtering.

nodes.title: Function calling in the OpenAI API
nodes.authors: OpenAI
nodes.before: Developers coaxed structured tool calls out of models with prompt templates and regex parsing.
nodes.problem: Free-text tool calls are unreliable to parse and break silently.
nodes.breakthrough: Declare functions with a JSON schema; the model returns a structured call the runtime can execute.
nodes.why: It turned agents from a research pattern into ordinary application development.
nodes.next: MCP standardised the connection between models and tools a year later.
nodes.inherits: Structured tool calling as a basic API feature.

nodes.title: Textbooks Are All You Need
nodes.authors: S. Gunasekar, Y. Zhang, J. Aneja, et al. (18 authors)
nodes.before: Capability was assumed to track parameters and raw token count.
nodes.problem: Web text is repetitive and much of it teaches the model very little.
nodes.breakthrough: Train a 1.3B model on a small corpus of textbook-quality and synthetic data, and beat far larger models at code.
nodes.why: It made data quality a first-class scaling variable and legitimised synthetic pretraining data.
nodes.next: The phi series, and synthetic data pipelines across the industry.
nodes.inherits: Curated and synthetic data as a substitute for raw scale.

nodes.title: Extending Context Window of Large Language Models via Positional Interpolation
nodes.authors: S. Chen, S. Wong, L. Chen, Y. Tian
nodes.before: A model trained at 2K tokens broke down badly past that length.
nodes.problem: Retraining from scratch at longer context is prohibitively expensive.
nodes.breakthrough: Scale RoPE position indices down to fit the trained range, then fine-tune briefly. 32K context from a 2K model in a thousand steps.
nodes.why: It made long context an affordable post-hoc upgrade rather than a training-time commitment.
nodes.next: YaRN and LongRoPE refined it; nearly every long-context open model uses some variant.
nodes.inherits: Context extension as a cheap fine-tuning step.

nodes.title: Lost in the Middle: How Language Models Use Long Contexts
nodes.authors: N. Liu, K. Lin, J. Hewitt, A. Paranjape, M. Bevilacqua, F. Petroni, P. Liang
nodes.before: Longer context windows were assumed to mean more usable information.
nodes.problem: Nobody had checked whether models actually use the middle of a long prompt.
nodes.breakthrough: Accuracy is high when the relevant passage is at the start or end and sags badly in the middle, in a U-shaped curve.
nodes.why: It explains why stuffing everything into context underperforms good retrieval, and why reranking still matters.
nodes.next: Better long-context training and evaluation, and continued investment in retrieval.
nodes.inherits: The knowledge that context position affects whether information is used.

nodes.title: Llama 2: Open Foundation and Fine-Tuned Chat Models
nodes.authors: H. Touvron, L. Martin, K. Stone, et al.
nodes.before: The best open weights were research-only, so companies could not build on them.
nodes.problem: Open models were a research curiosity rather than a commercial option.
nodes.breakthrough: Open weights with a commercial licence, a documented RLHF pipeline, and chat models tuned for safety.
nodes.why: It made open weights a viable business decision and set off serious enterprise adoption.
nodes.next: Code Llama, Llama 3 and 3.1, then the pivot away from open releases in 2026.
nodes.inherits: The community licence model, restrictions and all.

nodes.title: Efficient Memory Management for LLM Serving with PagedAttention
nodes.authors: W. Kwon, Z. Li, S. Zhuang, et al. (9 authors)
nodes.before: Serving systems reserved a contiguous block of memory per request for the KV cache.
nodes.problem: Requests vary in length, so most of that reserved memory sat unused while other requests queued.
nodes.breakthrough: Manage the KV cache in pages like virtual memory, so blocks are allocated on demand and shared between requests.
nodes.why: Two to four times the throughput at the same cost, and it became the default open serving engine.
nodes.next: The standard deployment path for open models, including the largest MoE models.
nodes.inherits: Paged KV cache and continuous batching in production serving.

nodes.title: GPT-4V(ision) System Card
nodes.authors: OpenAI
nodes.before: GPT-4 had image capability described in its report but not released.
nodes.problem: Vision raises distinct safety questions, from face recognition to CAPTCHA solving.
nodes.breakthrough: A public vision-capable assistant, shipped with a system card documenting the refusals and mitigations.
nodes.why: It made multimodal input an everyday feature and set expectations for how visual capability gets released.
nodes.next: GPT-4o folded vision, audio and text into one model.
nodes.inherits: Images as ordinary input to an assistant.

nodes.title: Mistral 7B
nodes.authors: A. Jiang, A. Sablayrolles, A. Mensch, et al.
nodes.before: Open models came from large US labs under restrictive or custom licences.
nodes.problem: Could a small model with good engineering beat a much larger one, under a fully permissive licence?
nodes.breakthrough: 7B with grouped-query and sliding-window attention, beating Llama 2 13B on every benchmark, Apache 2.0.
nodes.why: It reset expectations about what a small model can do and made Apache-licensed weights competitive.
nodes.next: Mixtral's open MoE, and a European frontier lab.
nodes.inherits: The efficient small open model as a serious deployment target.

nodes.title: SWE-bench: Can Language Models Resolve Real-World GitHub Issues?
nodes.authors: C. Jimenez, J. Yang, A. Wettig, S. Yao, K. Pei, O. Press, K. Narasimhan
nodes.before: Code benchmarks asked for self-contained functions judged by unit tests.
nodes.problem: Real engineering means navigating a repository and editing several files, which HumanEval does not test.
nodes.breakthrough: Real GitHub issues with their real test suites. The best model of the day resolved under 2%.
nodes.why: It gave agents a hard, honest target, and became the number every coding model is now judged on.
nodes.next: SWE-agent, Devin, and the climb past 80% by late 2025.
nodes.inherits: Repository-level task completion as the measure of an agent.

nodes.title: Mamba: Linear-Time Sequence Modeling with Selective State Spaces
nodes.authors: A. Gu, T. Dao
nodes.before: Attention's quadratic cost was treated as the price of good sequence modelling.
nodes.problem: State-space models scale linearly but could not match transformers on language.
nodes.breakthrough: Make the state-space parameters input-dependent, so the model can selectively remember or forget, with a hardware-aware scan.
nodes.why: The strongest challenger to attention so far. Frontier models remain transformers, so treat this as a live parallel branch.
nodes.next: Mamba-2 and hybrid attention-SSM architectures.
nodes.inherits: An open question about whether attention is the final answer.

nodes.title: Gemini: A Family of Highly Capable Multimodal Models
nodes.authors: Gemini Team, Google
nodes.before: Multimodality was added to text models afterwards, by bolting on an encoder.
nodes.problem: A bolted-on encoder limits how deeply modalities can interact.
nodes.breakthrough: A model family trained on text, images, audio and video from the start, across three sizes.
nodes.why: It established native multimodality as the frontier design and put Google back in direct competition.
nodes.next: Gemini 1.5's million-token context, then the 2.5 and 3 generations.
nodes.inherits: Natively multimodal training rather than adapter bridges.

nodes.title: Mixtral of Experts
nodes.authors: A. Jiang, A. Sablayrolles, A. Roux, et al.
nodes.before: Mixture-of-experts models were built and kept inside large labs.
nodes.problem: Nobody outside those labs could study or deploy a sparse model.
nodes.breakthrough: An open sparse MoE, 47B total parameters with about 13B active per token, matching much larger dense models.
nodes.why: It brought MoE into the open ecosystem and made the total-versus-active parameter distinction common knowledge.
nodes.next: DeepSeekMoE, Llama 4, Kimi and the open MoE era.
nodes.inherits: Sparse open models as a normal deployment option.

nodes.title: DeepSeek LLM: Scaling Open-Source Language Models with Longtermism
nodes.authors: DeepSeek-AI
nodes.before: Scaling laws were published by Western labs and taken on trust by everyone else.
nodes.problem: The published coefficients did not transfer cleanly to other data and hyperparameter regimes.
nodes.breakthrough: Their own scaling study on their own data, used to size 7B and 67B open models.
nodes.why: The opening move of the lab that would later ship R1 and V3, and a reminder that scaling laws are data-dependent.
nodes.next: DeepSeekMoE, DeepSeekMath and the V2 and V3 architectures.
nodes.inherits: Scaling laws as something you measure for your own setup.

nodes.title: DeepSeekMoE: Towards Ultimate Expert Specialization
nodes.authors: D. Dai, C. Deng, C. Zhao, et al. (17 authors)
nodes.before: MoE models used a handful of large experts with top-k routing.
nodes.problem: Coarse experts duplicate common knowledge and specialise poorly.
nodes.breakthrough: Many finer-grained experts plus a few always-on shared experts to hold common knowledge.
nodes.why: The architecture behind DeepSeek V2, V3 and R1, and the most copied MoE design of the current era.
nodes.next: DeepSeek-V2's latent attention, then V3 and R1.
nodes.inherits: Fine-grained plus shared experts as the modern MoE layout.

nodes.title: Dolma: an Open Corpus of Three Trillion Tokens
nodes.authors: L. Soldaini, et al.
nodes.before: Open corpora existed but the pipelines that produced them were partly undocumented.
nodes.problem: Without the tooling and decisions, you cannot audit or rebuild a corpus.
nodes.breakthrough: Three trillion tokens released with the full curation toolkit and documented design decisions.
nodes.why: It made pretraining data auditable, which matters for bias, contamination and copyright questions.
nodes.next: OLMo trained on it; FineWeb pushed the open-data quality bar further.
nodes.inherits: Data provenance as a publishable artefact.

nodes.title: OLMo: Accelerating the Science of Language Models
nodes.authors: D. Groeneveld, I. Beltagy, P. Walsh, et al. (43 authors)
nodes.before: Open-weight models shipped weights but withheld data, code and logs.
nodes.problem: Weights alone do not let you reproduce or diagnose how a model came to be.
nodes.breakthrough: Weights, data, training code, evaluation harness and intermediate checkpoints, all released.
nodes.why: The clearest example of genuinely open-source rather than merely open-weight, and the reference for that distinction.
nodes.next: OLMo 2 and 3, and continued pressure on what open should mean.
nodes.inherits: The vocabulary distinction between open weights and open source.

nodes.title: DeepSeekMath: Pushing the Limits of Mathematical Reasoning
nodes.authors: Z. Shao, P. Wang, Q. Zhu, et al. (11 authors)
nodes.before: RL fine-tuning used PPO, which needs a separate value network alongside the policy.
nodes.problem: The value model doubles memory and is the fiddliest part of the pipeline to stabilise.
nodes.breakthrough: Group Relative Policy Optimization: sample a group of answers and use their relative scores as the baseline, dropping the critic entirely.
nodes.why: GRPO is what made large-scale RL for reasoning affordable, and it is the algorithm behind DeepSeek-R1.
nodes.next: DeepSeek-V3's post-training, then R1, then wide adoption across open reasoning models.
nodes.inherits: The RL algorithm most open reasoning training now uses.

nodes.title: Gemini 1.5
nodes.authors: Google DeepMind
nodes.before: Long context in production meant 100K to 200K tokens.
nodes.problem: Codebases, film and long archives still did not fit, so everything needed chunking.
nodes.breakthrough: A sparse MoE model with a one-million-token context, retrieving accurately across the whole window.
nodes.why: It changed what people thought context length could be, and reopened the retrieval-versus-context argument.
nodes.next: Gemini 2.0 and 2.5; long context became a standard competitive axis.
nodes.inherits: Million-token context as an available option.

nodes.title: Gemma: Open Models Based on Gemini Research and Technology
nodes.authors: Gemma Team
nodes.before: Google published research and shipped products, but released no competitive open weights.
nodes.problem: The open ecosystem was consolidating around Meta and Mistral.
nodes.breakthrough: Small open models built from the Gemini work, under Google's own use-restricted terms.
nodes.why: It brought the third major lab into open weights and intensified the small-model competition.
nodes.next: Gemma 2 and 3, and continued pressure at the small end.
nodes.inherits: Frontier labs releasing small open models alongside closed flagships.

nodes.title: The Claude 3 model family
nodes.authors: Anthropic
nodes.before: GPT-4 had held the frontier alone for a year.
nodes.problem: No competitor had matched it across the board, and one model size fits no one.
nodes.breakthrough: Three sizes with a shared capability profile, vision input and 200K context, with Opus matching or beating GPT-4.
nodes.why: It ended GPT-4's uncontested lead and made tiered model families the standard product shape.
nodes.next: Claude 3.5 Sonnet showed a mid-tier could beat the previous flagship.
nodes.inherits: The small, medium, large family with one interface.

nodes.title: Chatbot Arena: An Open Platform for Evaluating LLMs by Human Preference
nodes.authors: W. Chiang, L. Zheng, Y. Sheng, et al.
nodes.before: Models were ranked on static benchmarks that leaked into training data.
nodes.problem: Benchmark scores stopped predicting which model people actually preferred.
nodes.breakthrough: Anonymous head-to-head comparisons from the public, aggregated into an Elo-style rating.
nodes.why: It became the field's de facto leaderboard, and exposed how weakly benchmark scores track usefulness.
nodes.next: Style controls and category breakdowns as the arena's own biases became apparent.
nodes.inherits: Human preference as the headline ranking, with all its noise.

nodes.title: Devin
nodes.authors: Cognition
nodes.before: Coding assistants completed code inside an editor while a human drove.
nodes.problem: Real tasks span many files, a terminal, a browser and several debugging cycles.
nodes.breakthrough: An agent with its own shell, editor and browser, taking a ticket and working it end to end. 13.86% on SWE-bench unassisted.
nodes.why: It defined the autonomous software engineer category, for both the investment wave and the scepticism.
nodes.next: SWE-agent published the open equivalent weeks later; Claude Code and Codex productised it in 2025.
nodes.inherits: The agent with its own computer as the shape of AI coding.

nodes.title: Llama 3
nodes.authors: Meta AI
nodes.before: Llama 2 had been trained on two trillion tokens.
nodes.problem: Chinchilla-optimal training leaves inference-time performance on the table for a model you serve constantly.
nodes.breakthrough: 8B and 70B models trained on fifteen trillion tokens, far past the compute-optimal point.
nodes.why: Overtraining for inference efficiency became the open-model norm, and these were the first widely deployed examples.
nodes.next: Llama 3.1 added the 405B model and 128K context.
nodes.inherits: Train small models for much longer than compute-optimal.

nodes.title: Phi-3 Technical Report
nodes.authors: M. Abdin, et al.
nodes.before: Small models were assumed to be weak, and useful mainly for cheap tasks.
nodes.problem: Phones and laptops cannot run a 70B model, but their users want capable assistance.
nodes.breakthrough: A 3.8B model trained on heavily filtered and synthetic data, performing near models ten times its size.
nodes.why: It pushed the data-quality thesis to its edge and made on-device assistants credible.
nodes.next: The phi series continued; every lab now ships a small model tuned on synthetic data.
nodes.inherits: On-device capability through data curation rather than scale.

nodes.title: DeepSeek-V2: A Strong, Economical, and Efficient Mixture-of-Experts Language Model
nodes.authors: DeepSeek-AI
nodes.before: Grouped-query attention was the standard way to shrink the KV cache.
nodes.problem: Even grouped keys and values dominate memory during long-context inference.
nodes.breakthrough: Multi-head latent attention: compress keys and values into a low-rank latent vector and cache that instead.
nodes.why: A far larger cache reduction than GQA, and the reason DeepSeek could serve long context so cheaply.
nodes.next: DeepSeek-V3 and R1 use it; later sparse attention built on top.
nodes.inherits: Latent KV compression as the current frontier of inference efficiency.

nodes.title: SWE-agent: Agent-Computer Interfaces Enable Automated Software Engineering
nodes.authors: J. Yang, C. Jimenez, A. Wettig, et al. (7 authors)
nodes.before: Agents were given raw shell access and expected to cope.
nodes.problem: Interfaces built for humans are poor interfaces for models, which have no screen and limited context.
nodes.breakthrough: Design the interface for the agent: scoped file viewing, guarded edits with linting, and concise feedback.
nodes.why: It showed a large share of agent performance comes from interface design rather than model capability.
nodes.next: The agent-computer interface idea runs through every serious coding agent since.
nodes.inherits: Tool design as a first-class part of agent engineering.

nodes.title: GPT-4o
nodes.authors: OpenAI
nodes.before: Voice assistants chained speech recognition, a text model and speech synthesis.
nodes.problem: That chain adds seconds of latency and discards tone, emotion and overlapping speech.
nodes.breakthrough: One model trained across text, audio and vision, responding to audio in about 320 milliseconds on average.
nodes.why: It made real-time spoken conversation with a model possible, and set the native-multimodal expectation.
nodes.next: Realtime APIs, and native multimodality across the frontier.
nodes.inherits: One model for all modalities rather than a pipeline.

nodes.title: Claude 3.5 Sonnet
nodes.authors: Anthropic
nodes.before: Capability tracked size, so the flagship was always the largest model.
nodes.problem: The largest model is also the slowest and most expensive to serve.
nodes.breakthrough: A mid-tier model outperforming the previous flagship at a fraction of the cost and latency.
nodes.why: It broke the assumption that frontier capability requires frontier size, and made strong models cheap enough for agents to call repeatedly.
nodes.next: The 3.5 line gained computer use in October, then 3.7 added extended thinking.
nodes.inherits: Cheap frontier-class models as the substrate for agent loops.

nodes.title: The FineWeb Datasets: Decanting the Web for the Finest Text Data at Scale
nodes.authors: G. Penedo, H. Kydlíček, L. Ben Allal, et al. (8 authors)
nodes.before: Data recipes were described in papers but rarely released with their ablations.
nodes.problem: Everyone rebuilt the same filtering pipeline and could not compare choices.
nodes.breakthrough: Fifteen trillion tokens plus the ablation study behind every filtering decision, and an education-filtered subset.
nodes.why: It made data curation an open empirical science, and FineWeb-Edu showed filtering for educational value beats raw volume.
nodes.next: The standard open pretraining corpus for new model efforts.
nodes.inherits: Published ablations as part of a dataset release.

nodes.title: FlashAttention-3: Fast and Accurate Attention with Asynchrony and Low-precision
nodes.authors: J. Shah, G. Bikshandi, Y. Zhang, et al. (6 authors)
nodes.before: FlashAttention-2 was tuned for the previous GPU generation.
nodes.problem: Hopper GPUs have asynchronous copy engines and FP8 units that the older kernel left idle.
nodes.breakthrough: Overlap computation with data movement and exploit low precision, roughly doubling attention throughput on H100s.
nodes.why: Attention kernels are now co-designed with each GPU generation, and this is the current reference implementation.
nodes.next: Folded into serving stacks and the training runs of most 2024 and 2025 models.
nodes.inherits: Hardware-specific attention kernels as standard infrastructure.

nodes.title: Qwen2 Technical Report
nodes.authors: A. Yang et al. (Qwen Team)
nodes.before: Open weights meant Western labs, with English-centric training data.
nodes.problem: Most of the world's users and much of its text are not English.
nodes.breakthrough: A full family from 0.5B to 72B with strong multilingual coverage, mostly Apache 2.0.
nodes.why: Qwen became the most downloaded and fine-tuned open family, and the base for a large share of derivative models.
nodes.next: Qwen2.5, Qwen3 and the 2026 releases.
nodes.inherits: A genuinely multilingual open baseline.

nodes.title: The Llama 3 Herd of Models
nodes.authors: Meta AI (Grattafiori, Dubey et al.)
nodes.before: Open weights trailed the closed frontier by a clear margin.
nodes.problem: Nobody had released a model that could stand beside GPT-4 class systems.
nodes.breakthrough: 405B parameters, 128K context, a candid 90-page account of the training, and a licence permitting distillation from outputs.
nodes.why: Open weights reached the frontier, and the distillation clause seeded a generation of smaller models.
nodes.next: Llama 4's MoE in 2025, then Meta's pivot to closed models in 2026.
nodes.inherits: The expectation that open weights compete at the frontier, now contested.

nodes.title: Scaling LLM Test-Time Compute Optimally
nodes.authors: C. Snell, J. Lee, K. Xu, A. Kumar
nodes.before: Scaling meant training compute: more parameters, more data.
nodes.problem: Nobody had systematically compared spending compute at training time against spending it at inference.
nodes.breakthrough: A compute-optimal analysis of inference strategies, showing extra thinking can beat a much larger model on some problems.
nodes.why: It gave the reasoning-model era its theoretical footing, weeks before o1 shipped.
nodes.next: o1 and o3, then DeepSeek-R1 and the open reasoning models.
nodes.inherits: Inference compute as a second scaling axis.

nodes.title: OpenAI o1
nodes.authors: OpenAI
nodes.before: Reasoning was prompted at inference time with chain-of-thought.
nodes.problem: Prompted reasoning is shallow, easily derailed, and not something the model was trained to do well.
nodes.breakthrough: Train the model with reinforcement learning to produce long internal reasoning before answering, and let it spend more tokens on harder problems.
nodes.why: It opened a second scaling axis and reset the field's direction. OpenAI disclosed no architecture or parameters, and hides the reasoning tokens.
nodes.next: o3 in December, then DeepSeek-R1 replicated the idea openly in January.
nodes.inherits: Reasoning trained in rather than prompted for.

nodes.title: Claude computer use
nodes.authors: Anthropic
nodes.before: Agents acted through APIs and function calls, so they could only use software that offered one.
nodes.problem: Most software has no API. It has a screen, a mouse and a keyboard.
nodes.breakthrough: The model looks at screenshots and moves the cursor, clicks and types like a person.
nodes.why: It removed the API precondition for automation and started the computer-use agent line across all major labs.
nodes.next: OpenAI's Operator, Gemini's agentic modes, and the 2026 computer-using coding agents.
nodes.inherits: The screen as a universal interface for agents.

nodes.title: Model Context Protocol
nodes.authors: Anthropic
nodes.before: Every tool integration was written per model and per application.
nodes.problem: Connecting M models to N tools means M times N bespoke integrations.
nodes.breakthrough: An open protocol for exposing tools, data and prompts to any model, so each side implements it once.
nodes.why: It turned tool connectivity into shared infrastructure, and was adopted across the industry within a year.
nodes.next: Adopted by other labs and the agent tooling ecosystem through 2025 and 2026.
nodes.inherits: A common protocol between models and the systems they act on.

nodes.title: Gemini 2.0
nodes.authors: Google DeepMind
nodes.before: Multimodal models took images and audio in, and emitted text.
nodes.problem: Agents need models that also act, natively call tools and produce other modalities.
nodes.breakthrough: A model built for the agentic era, with native tool use, multimodal output and experimental thinking modes.
nodes.why: It marked Google's reorientation from chat assistant to agent platform.
nodes.next: Gemini 2.5's thinking models, then Gemini 3.
nodes.inherits: Native tool use as a model capability rather than a wrapper.

nodes.title: OpenAI o3 announcement
nodes.authors: OpenAI
nodes.before: o1 had established RL-trained reasoning three months earlier.
nodes.problem: Was the approach a one-off, or does reasoning keep improving with more RL and more inference compute?
nodes.breakthrough: Large jumps on ARC-AGI and FrontierMath, at very high inference cost per task.
nodes.why: It showed the reasoning axis had real headroom. Note the scores are OpenAI-reported, ARC-AGI results are on the public eval set, and Epoch AI later disclosed OpenAI funding and data access for FrontierMath.
nodes.next: Released in April 2025 alongside o4-mini, then folded into GPT-5.
nodes.inherits: Reasoning capability that scales with inference spend, and the cost question that comes with it.

nodes.title: DeepSeek-V3 Technical Report
nodes.authors: DeepSeek-AI
nodes.before: Frontier training was assumed to cost hundreds of millions of dollars.
nodes.problem: Export controls limited Chinese labs to slower H800 GPUs, so efficiency was forced rather than chosen.
nodes.breakthrough: 671B parameters with 37B active, combining latent attention and fine-grained MoE, trained in 2.788M GPU-hours.
nodes.why: Frontier-class results at a reported 5.576 million dollars for the final run. Note that figure excludes all prior research and failed runs.
nodes.next: R1 was built on this base a month later and reset expectations about open reasoning.
nodes.inherits: The efficiency-first frontier model, and a permanent argument about training costs.

nodes.title: DeepSeek-R1: Incentivizing Reasoning Capability in LLMs via Reinforcement Learning
nodes.authors: DeepSeek-AI
nodes.before: o1 had shown RL-trained reasoning worked, with no published method.
nodes.problem: Nobody outside OpenAI knew whether it needed vast supervised reasoning data or some undisclosed trick.
nodes.breakthrough: Reasoning emerged from reinforcement learning alone, with no supervised cold start, using GRPO on a V3 base. Weights released under MIT.
nodes.why: It replicated the reasoning paradigm openly and cheaply, and became the first frontier LLM result peer-reviewed in Nature.
nodes.next: Open reasoning models across Qwen, Kimi and GLM, and distilled reasoning into small models.
nodes.inherits: Reasoning as something you can train yourself, with a published recipe.

nodes.title: Deep research
nodes.authors: OpenAI
nodes.before: Search-augmented answers came back in seconds from a handful of pages.
nodes.problem: Real research means dozens of sources, cross-checking and a written synthesis, which does not fit in one turn.
nodes.breakthrough: A reasoning model given browsing and many minutes to work, producing a cited report.
nodes.why: It made long-running autonomous research a mainstream product feature, copied by every major lab within months.
nodes.next: Equivalent modes in Gemini, Claude and Perplexity.
nodes.inherits: Agents that run for minutes rather than seconds.

nodes.title: Claude 3.7 Sonnet
nodes.authors: Anthropic
nodes.before: Reasoning models were a separate product line from chat models.
nodes.problem: Users had to pick the right model, and reasoning cost applied even to trivial questions.
nodes.breakthrough: One model with an extended thinking mode you can switch on, and a visible budget for how long it thinks.
nodes.why: The hybrid design became the industry pattern, ending the split between chat and reasoning models.
nodes.next: GPT-5's router and Gemini 2.5's thinking models followed the same logic.
nodes.inherits: Reasoning as a dial on a single model.

nodes.title: Claude Code
nodes.authors: Anthropic
nodes.before: AI coding lived in the editor as completions and chat. Devin and SWE-agent had shown the agent form a year earlier.
nodes.problem: Editor plugins cannot run tests, read a repository or iterate until something works.
nodes.breakthrough: An agent in the terminal with the repository, the shell and the test suite, working a task for many turns.
nodes.why: It made agentic coding a daily professional tool rather than a demo, and defined the terminal-agent form factor.
nodes.next: OpenAI's Codex agent, Gemini's Antigravity and the 2026 computer-using coding agents.
nodes.inherits: The coding agent as standard developer tooling.

nodes.title: GPT-4.5
nodes.authors: OpenAI
nodes.before: Each generation had come from more pretraining scale.
nodes.problem: Was there still headroom in scaling pretraining alone, now that reasoning was the growth area?
nodes.breakthrough: OpenAI's largest pretraining scale-up, positioned on warmth and fewer hallucinations rather than reasoning.
nodes.why: Read in hindsight as the end of the pure-pretraining era. It was retired within months as the reasoning line took over.
nodes.next: GPT-5 unified the reasoning and chat lines instead of scaling pretraining further.
nodes.inherits: A datapoint on the diminishing returns of pretraining scale alone.

nodes.title: Gemini 2.5
nodes.authors: Google DeepMind
nodes.before: Thinking was an experimental mode on one model variant.
nodes.problem: If reasoning helps broadly, it should not be a special case.
nodes.breakthrough: Thinking built into every model in the family by default, with long context retained.
nodes.why: It made reasoning table stakes rather than a premium tier, across a whole product line.
nodes.next: Gemini 3 and the Deep Think variants.
nodes.inherits: Reasoning on by default.

nodes.title: Llama 4
nodes.authors: Meta AI
nodes.before: Llama models were dense and text-first.
nodes.problem: Dense models had become uncompetitive on cost against the open MoE models coming out of China.
nodes.breakthrough: Meta's first mixture-of-experts models, natively multimodal, with very long advertised context.
nodes.why: It brought Meta into the MoE era, and turned out to be the last open Llama generation.
nodes.next: Meta pivoted to the closed Muse Spark line in April 2026.
nodes.inherits: MoE as the default frontier architecture, open or closed.

nodes.title: OpenAI o3
nodes.authors: OpenAI
nodes.before: o1 reasoned in a closed loop with no access to anything outside itself.
nodes.problem: Reasoning without tools cannot look anything up or run code to check itself.
nodes.breakthrough: A reasoning model that calls tools, including search and code execution, inside its chain of thought.
nodes.why: Reasoning and tool use merged here, which is the technical basis of the agentic models that followed.
nodes.next: Folded into GPT-5's unified system later that year.
nodes.inherits: Tool calls inside the reasoning loop.

nodes.title: OpenAI o4-mini
nodes.authors: OpenAI
nodes.before: Reasoning models were expensive enough to reserve for hard problems.
nodes.problem: Agents make many calls, so per-call reasoning cost compounds badly.
nodes.breakthrough: A small reasoning model cheap enough to call repeatedly, with tool use.
nodes.why: Cheap reasoning is what makes long agent loops economically possible.
nodes.next: The same logic drives the mini and flash tiers across all labs.
nodes.inherits: Reasoning at a price point agents can afford.

nodes.title: Qwen3
nodes.authors: Qwen Team
nodes.before: Open models shipped either as chat models or as separate reasoning variants.
nodes.problem: Maintaining two lines doubles the work and confuses deployment.
nodes.breakthrough: One family from 0.6B to 235B with switchable thinking and non-thinking modes.
nodes.why: It brought the hybrid reasoning design to open weights across every size class.
nodes.next: Qwen3.5 and the 2026 releases.
nodes.inherits: Hybrid reasoning in models you can download.

nodes.title: Claude 4 (Opus 4 and Sonnet 4)
nodes.authors: Anthropic
nodes.before: Coding agents worked in short bursts and lost the thread on longer tasks.
nodes.problem: Real engineering tasks run for hours and require holding context across many steps.
nodes.breakthrough: Hybrid reasoning models tuned for sustained agentic work, reported at 72.5% on SWE-bench Verified.
nodes.why: It set the agentic coding bar for the year and made multi-hour autonomous tasks a selling point. The benchmark figures are vendor-reported.
nodes.next: The 4.5 line in late 2025, then Claude 5 in 2026.
nodes.inherits: Long-horizon agentic work as the thing frontier models compete on.

nodes.title: Kimi K2
nodes.authors: Kimi Team
nodes.before: Open MoE models topped out well below a trillion parameters.
nodes.problem: Training at that scale is unstable, and agentic skill needs data nobody had assembled.
nodes.breakthrough: A roughly one-trillion-parameter open MoE with about 32B active, trained with the MuonClip optimizer and heavy agentic post-training.
nodes.why: Open weights reached trillion-parameter scale with agentic capability, from outside the established labs.
nodes.next: Kimi K3 in 2026 took it to multimodal at a larger scale.
nodes.inherits: Trillion-parameter open models as a real category.

nodes.title: IMO gold-medal performance
nodes.authors: OpenAI; Google DeepMind
nodes.before: Models solved competition problems only with formal tools or heavy scaffolding.
nodes.problem: Olympiad problems need original proofs written in natural language under time limits.
nodes.breakthrough: Two labs independently scored 35 of 42, solving five of six problems, in natural language. DeepMind's run was certified by IMO coordinators.
nodes.why: A milestone for mathematical reasoning, though later independent evaluation found much weaker performance on unfamiliar problems.
nodes.next: IMO-ProofBench and other independent evaluations testing generalisation.
nodes.inherits: Both the achievement and the caution about what benchmark scores mean.

nodes.title: gpt-oss-120b and gpt-oss-20b
nodes.authors: OpenAI
nodes.before: OpenAI had released no open weights since GPT-2 in 2019.
nodes.problem: The open ecosystem had consolidated around Meta and Chinese labs, with no US frontier lab participating.
nodes.breakthrough: Two open-weight reasoning models under Apache 2.0, trained with techniques from the o-series.
nodes.why: It reversed a six-year position and put a US frontier lab back in the open ecosystem.
nodes.next: Continued competition with Qwen, DeepSeek and Kimi at the open end.
nodes.inherits: Open weights as something every major lab now has a position on.

nodes.title: GPT-5
nodes.authors: OpenAI
nodes.before: Users chose between a fast chat model and a slow reasoning model, and mostly chose wrong.
nodes.problem: Model selection is a burden users should not carry and cannot do well.
nodes.breakthrough: A unified system with a router that decides per request how much reasoning to spend.
nodes.why: It ended the model-picker era and made reasoning depth an automatic decision rather than a user's.
nodes.next: The 5.1 through 5.6 point releases through 2026.
nodes.inherits: Routing between capability tiers behind one name.

nodes.title: GLM-4.5
nodes.authors: GLM team
nodes.before: Open agentic models came mainly from DeepSeek, Qwen and Moonshot.
nodes.problem: Reasoning, coding and agentic skill were usually strong in one model and weak in the others.
nodes.breakthrough: An open MoE explicitly targeting all three together, released under MIT.
nodes.why: It widened the open frontier to a fourth serious lab and pushed the unified-capability framing.
nodes.inherits: Open models competing on agentic benchmarks, not just knowledge.

nodes.title: Claude Sonnet 4.5
nodes.authors: Anthropic
nodes.before: Opus 4 led on coding and computer use.
nodes.problem: Frontier coding capability was priced out of reach for continuous agent use.
nodes.breakthrough: A mid-tier model reported at 77.2% on SWE-bench Verified, ahead of the previous flagship.
nodes.why: It continued the pattern of frontier capability arriving at mid-tier prices, which is what makes agents affordable.
nodes.next: Opus 4.5 passed 80% two months later.
nodes.inherits: Falling cost per unit of agentic capability.

nodes.title: DeepSeek-V3.2 with DeepSeek Sparse Attention
nodes.authors: DeepSeek-AI
nodes.before: Latent attention had reduced the KV cache, but attention cost still grew with length.
nodes.problem: Long-context inference remained expensive per token as sequences grew.
nodes.breakthrough: A trainable sparse attention mechanism that selects which past tokens to attend to, cutting long-context cost sharply.
nodes.why: It revived sparse attention as a frontier technique rather than a compromise, and cut long-context prices.
nodes.next: DeepSeek V4's million-token context in 2026.
nodes.inherits: Learned sparsity as the current answer to long-context cost.

nodes.title: Towards Robust Mathematical Reasoning (IMO-ProofBench)
nodes.authors: Luong et al., Google DeepMind
nodes.before: Gold-medal olympiad results were taken as evidence of general mathematical reasoning.
nodes.problem: Competition problems and their solutions circulate widely, so scores may reflect familiarity rather than reasoning.
nodes.breakthrough: A proof benchmark with novel problems, on which most models fell far below their headline results.
nodes.why: The clearest independent check on the year's most-cited reasoning claims, and a caution for reading any vendor benchmark.
nodes.next: More emphasis on contamination-resistant evaluation.
nodes.inherits: Scepticism as a standard part of reading capability claims.

nodes.title: GPT-5.1
nodes.authors: OpenAI
nodes.before: GPT-5's router applied a fixed reasoning policy.
nodes.problem: Reasoning effort should track problem difficulty more finely than a router decides.
nodes.breakthrough: Adaptive reasoning effort and a coding-specialised Codex-Max variant.
nodes.why: Part of the shift to rapid point releases as the competitive cadence.
nodes.next: GPT-5.2 a month later, then the 2026 series.
nodes.inherits: Monthly-cadence frontier updates.

nodes.title: Gemini 3
nodes.authors: Google DeepMind
nodes.before: OpenAI and Anthropic had traded the frontier between them through 2025.
nodes.problem: Google's earlier generations trailed on agentic and coding work.
nodes.breakthrough: A frontier multimodal reasoning model with an agentic development platform alongside it.
nodes.why: It put Google clearly back at the frontier and reportedly triggered an internal emergency response at OpenAI.
nodes.next: Gemini 3 Deep Think and 3.1 in early 2026.
nodes.inherits: A genuinely three-way frontier race.

nodes.title: Claude Opus 4.5
nodes.authors: Anthropic
nodes.before: SWE-bench Verified scores had been climbing through the 70s all year.
nodes.problem: Whether agents could reliably resolve most real issues was still open.
nodes.breakthrough: 80.9% on SWE-bench Verified, the first model reported above 80, at a lower price than its predecessor.
nodes.why: The 80% mark was the year's psychological threshold for agentic coding. The figure is vendor-reported with its own scaffold.
nodes.next: The Claude 5 generation in 2026.
nodes.inherits: Agentic coding as the headline capability measure.

nodes.title: GPT-5.2
nodes.authors: OpenAI
nodes.before: Gemini 3 had taken several benchmark leads in November.
nodes.problem: Competitive response now has to arrive in weeks, not generations.
nodes.breakthrough: A fast follow-up release in the GPT-5 series.
nodes.why: It marks how short the frontier release cycle had become by the end of 2025.
nodes.next: GPT-5.3-Codex through 5.6 across 2026.
nodes.inherits: Point releases as the unit of frontier competition.

nodes.title: Claude Opus 4.6
nodes.authors: Anthropic
nodes.before: Opus 4.5 held the agentic coding lead.
nodes.problem: Competitors released on a monthly cadence.
nodes.breakthrough: Further agentic and coding improvements in the Opus line.
nodes.why: Part of the tight release cycle of early 2026.
nodes.next: Opus 4.7 and 4.8 followed within months.
nodes.inherits: Incremental frontier releases.

nodes.title: GPT-5.3-Codex
nodes.authors: OpenAI
nodes.before: Coding agents worked through the shell and the file system.
nodes.problem: Some development work happens in browsers and GUIs that have no command-line equivalent.
nodes.breakthrough: A coding model that also drives a computer directly.
nodes.why: It merged the coding-agent and computer-use lines into one product.
nodes.next: The GPT-5.4 and 5.5 releases continued the agentic push.
nodes.inherits: Coding agents that are not limited to the terminal.

nodes.title: Gemini 3 Deep Think
nodes.authors: Google DeepMind
nodes.before: Deep Think was the variant behind the 2025 olympiad result.
nodes.problem: That capability sat in a research configuration rather than a product.
nodes.breakthrough: A substantial upgrade to the deep reasoning mode, offered to subscribers.
nodes.why: It brought the heaviest reasoning configuration into general availability.
nodes.next: Gemini 3.1 the following week.
nodes.inherits: Maximum-effort reasoning as a purchasable tier.

nodes.title: Qwen3.5
nodes.authors: Qwen Team
nodes.before: Qwen3 was the widely used open baseline.
nodes.problem: Open models needed to keep pace with a frontier moving monthly.
nodes.breakthrough: A large sparse MoE release continuing the Apache-licensed family.
nodes.why: It kept a fully permissive open option close to the frontier.
nodes.next: Qwen3.6 and 3.8 later in 2026.
nodes.inherits: A permissively licensed open baseline that tracks the frontier.

nodes.title: Claude Sonnet 4.6
nodes.authors: Anthropic
nodes.before: Long context on the mid tier was capped at 200K tokens.
nodes.problem: Agents working across large repositories exhaust that quickly.
nodes.breakthrough: A mid-tier model with a million-token context in beta.
nodes.why: Long context reached the price tier that agents actually run on.
nodes.next: The Claude 5 generation mid-year.
nodes.inherits: Very long context at mid-tier prices.

nodes.title: Gemini 3.1 Pro

chapters.title: Language as probability
chapters.lede: Can you describe language well enough to predict it?
body: The story starts with a question from information theory rather than linguistics. In 1948 Claude Shannon treated English as a source of symbols and measured how predictable the next one was. For forty years afterwards, language models were counts: how often does this word follow those two? IBM used exactly that idea to translate text statistically, replacing hand-written grammar rules with probabilities learned from data.

Counting has a ceiling. Most sentences you will ever read have never been written before, so a model that only remembers sequences it has seen gives them zero probability. In 2003 Yoshua Bengio's group proposed learning a vector for every word, so that similar words share what the model knows about them. That single move, meaning as position in a learned space, is still inside every model today.
chapters.transition: The idea was right, but the computers were too slow to use it at scale. That changed a decade later.

chapters.title: Words become vectors
chapters.lede: What happens when learning word meanings becomes cheap?
body: In 2013 Tomas Mikolov's team at Google stripped Bengio's model down to almost nothing and trained it on billions of words in under a day. The resulting vectors had a famous property: the direction from man to woman was roughly the direction from king to queen. Meaning had geometry, and anyone could compute it.

The same period produced the other half of the modern recipe. Sequence-to-sequence models read a whole sentence with one recurrent network and wrote a translation with another, end to end. And subword tokenization solved the rare-word problem by spelling unfamiliar words out of pieces. By 2016 Google had put neural translation into production.
chapters.transition: There was a flaw at the centre of sequence-to-sequence: the whole input had to fit through one fixed-size vector.

chapters.title: Attention, then only attention
chapters.lede: What if the model could look back at the input instead of remembering it?
body: Squeezing a long sentence into one vector loses information, and translation quality fell apart on long inputs. In 2014 Dzmitry Bahdanau, working with Kyunghyun Cho and Yoshua Bengio, let the decoder look back over every input word and weight each by relevance. That mechanism is attention, and it starts here, three years before the paper with attention in its title.

In 2017 a Google team asked what would happen if attention were the only mechanism, with no recurrence at all. The answer was the Transformer. Its real advantage was not accuracy but parallelism: every position could be processed at once, which is exactly what GPUs are good at. That is what made the next decade of scaling affordable.
chapters.transition: The Transformer was built for translation. Within a year, two labs used it for something far more general.

chapters.title: Pretrain once, use everywhere
chapters.lede: Could one model learn language first, and tasks later?
body: Until 2018 most models were trained from scratch for one job. Then three ideas arrived within months of each other. ELMo showed that a language model's internal states make excellent word representations. OpenAI's GPT pretrained the Transformer's decoder on plain text by predicting the next word. Google's BERT pretrained the encoder by predicting masked words from both directions.

That fork matters. BERT dominated research for three years and still powers search and embeddings. GPT's next-word prediction looked like the weaker choice, until GPT-2 in 2019 showed that at 1.5 billion parameters it could translate, summarise and answer questions it was never trained on. T5 then reframed every task as text in, text out.
chapters.transition: GPT-2 suggested that size itself was doing the work. The next question was how much.

chapters.title: Scale becomes a science
chapters.lede: If bigger is better, how much better, and bigger in what?
body: In January 2020 OpenAI published scaling laws: a model's loss falls predictably as parameters, data and compute grow, across seven orders of magnitude. Scale stopped being a gamble and became a budget. Four months later GPT-3, at 175 billion parameters, showed something new: give it a few examples in the prompt and it does the task, with no retraining. Prompting was born.

In 2022 DeepMind's Chinchilla corrected the recipe. Everyone had grown models far faster than their data, so a 70-billion-parameter model trained on more text beat one four times its size. The lesson, scale data and parameters together, is why capable small models exist. The same year, researchers argued over whether some abilities appear suddenly at scale, or only look sudden because of how they are measured.
chapters.transition: GPT-3 was powerful and awkward. It continued your text rather than doing what you asked.

chapters.title: Teaching models what people want
chapters.lede: How do you train a model toward a goal you can judge but not write down?
body: The answer began outside language entirely. In 2017 researchers at OpenAI and DeepMind trained a reward model from human comparisons, asking which of two behaviours was better, and then optimised against it. By 2019 the same method was fine-tuning language models; by 2020 it produced summaries people preferred to human-written ones.

In 2022 InstructGPT applied it to instruction following. A 1.3-billion-parameter aligned model was preferred to the raw 175-billion one. That result is the key to this chapter: alignment does not add much knowledge. It steers and draws out what pretraining already put there. Anthropic then wrote the rules down as a constitution, and in 2023 DPO showed the whole reinforcement-learning loop could be replaced by a simple loss.
chapters.transition: By late 2022 the technique was mature. What it lacked was an audience.

chapters.title: The assistant goes public
chapters.lede: What changed when anyone could talk to one?
body: The first mass-market language model product was not a chatbot. GitHub Copilot put a code model inside developers' editors in mid-2021. But the inflection came on 30 November 2022, when OpenAI released ChatGPT, a free chat interface to the InstructGPT recipe. It reached an estimated hundred million users within about two months.

It is worth being precise about what ChatGPT was. It introduced no new capability; OpenAI described it as a sibling of InstructGPT. It was a breakthrough in interface and distribution. The capability jump came four months later with GPT-4, and Anthropic's Claude made the frontier a competition.
chapters.transition: From here the story splits. Several threads develop at once, so each of the next chapters follows one of them from its origin to the present.

chapters.title: The weights get out
chapters.lede: Who gets to run, study and change these models?
body: Until 2023 the best models lived behind APIs. Meta's LLaMA changed that in February 2023: small models, trained far longer than Chinchilla suggested, released to researchers. The weights leaked within days, and within weeks people had fine-tuned them into assistants for a few hundred dollars. Llama 2 added a commercial licence; Mistral showed a 7-billion-parameter model could beat far larger ones under a fully permissive licence.

Most of these are open-weight rather than open-source: you can download them, but custom licences restrict use and the training data is rarely released. By 2025 the open frontier had moved to DeepSeek, Qwen and Moonshot, and in 2026 Meta itself stopped releasing open models.
chapters.transition: Downloading a model is only useful if you can afford to run it.

chapters.title: Making it run anywhere
chapters.lede: How does a model built for a datacentre end up on a laptop?
body: A thread of efficiency work runs quietly under everything else. FlashAttention made attention fast by reorganising memory traffic rather than approximating the maths. Quantization shrank weights from 16 bits to 8 and then 4 with little loss. LoRA let you fine-tune a model by training a tiny adapter beside it, and QLoRA combined the two so a 65-billion-parameter model could be tuned on one GPU.

Serving changed too. vLLM managed the model's working memory like an operating system manages RAM, and throughput rose two to four times. llama.cpp ran models on ordinary CPUs. Most of what you would do to run a model locally today was invented in this stretch.
chapters.transition: Efficiency made models cheaper. It did not make them know more, or see more.

chapters.title: Reading more than you remember
chapters.lede: What should live in the model's weights, and what should it look up?
body: A model's knowledge is frozen at training time, cannot cite a source, and goes stale. In 2020 Facebook AI's RAG paired a generator with a retriever: embed the question, find relevant passages, and answer with them in view. That pattern, retrieval-augmented generation, now sits behind most production systems that answer questions about private or current information.

The alternative is to read everything at once. Context windows grew from about 2,000 tokens to 100,000 in 2023 and a million in 2024. But in 2023 researchers found models use the middle of a long context poorly, which is one reason good retrieval never went away.
chapters.transition: Text was never going to be the only input.

chapters.title: Seeing and hearing
chapters.lede: Can one model share a single understanding across images, sound and words?
body: The Vision Transformer cut images into patches and treated them as tokens, so one architecture could handle pixels and words. OpenAI's CLIP then trained image and text encoders together on 400 million web pairs until matching pictures and captions landed in the same place. That shared space is the bridge every vision-language model crosses.

Early multimodal models bolted a vision encoder onto a language model. By 2023 Gemini was trained on several modalities from the start, and in 2024 GPT-4o answered spoken questions in about a third of a second by handling audio natively rather than chaining separate systems.
chapters.transition: Seeing more is one direction. Thinking longer is another.

chapters.title: Thinking longer
chapters.lede: What if a model spent more effort on harder questions?
body: In 2022 researchers found that showing a model worked examples, with the reasoning written out, made it reason step by step too. Sampling several reasoning paths and voting helped more. The implication took two years to land: computation at inference time can substitute for size.

In September 2024 OpenAI's o1 trained that behaviour in with reinforcement learning, producing long hidden reasoning before answering. In January 2025 DeepSeek-R1 reproduced the result openly, showing reasoning can emerge from reinforcement learning alone, and published the method. Within months every major lab offered a model that thinks before it answers.
chapters.transition: A model that can reason about a task can also start carrying it out.

chapters.title: Models that act
chapters.lede: What changes when the output is an action, not an answer?
body: In 2021 WebGPT gave a model a text browser and taught it to search and cite. In 2022 ReAct combined reasoning and acting into one loop: think, act, observe, repeat. Almost every agent since is built on that loop. In 2023 SWE-bench asked models to fix real GitHub issues; the best of the day solved under 2 percent.

Then the tooling caught up. Function calling made tool use a standard API feature, computer use let a model operate a screen, and the Model Context Protocol standardised how models connect to tools. Coding agents became everyday tools in 2025, and reported SWE-bench scores passed 80 percent, though those figures are vendor-reported.
chapters.transition: Which brings the threads back together, in the present.

chapters.title: Where the threads meet now
chapters.lede: What does a frontier model look like when every thread converges?
body: A 2026 frontier model is the sum of this route: a Transformer, pretrained on filtered web-scale data, aligned with preference optimisation, reasoning with reinforcement-learned chains of thought, reading long context and images, and calling tools as an agent. GPT-5's router made the reasoning depth automatic. Releases now arrive monthly.

Two things are new. Frontier models are increasingly released in tiers of access rather than simply published, and governments have become direct participants: the EU AI Act's obligations for general-purpose models applied from August 2026, and in June 2026 a US export-control directive briefly took a deployed model offline.
